The underlying language model parameters remain unchanged, and the framework does not rely on an additional mathematical solver, external symbolic engine, or task-specific finetuning procedure. Its only additional computation consists of the repeated guidance and reasoning generations. Consequently, SGR can be applied to general-purpose instruction-following language models using prompt-level modifications alone.

For fair comparison across models, the same overall procedure can be instantiated with each evaluated model, while model-specific restrictions are limited to the required input and output formats. The method is therefore compatible with models of different sizes and with both general-purpose and mathematics-oriented language models.

title: Step Guided Reasoning: Improving Mathematical Reasoning using Guidance Generation and Step Reasoning
text:
## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Setting

We evaluate Step Guided Reasoning as a training-free inference framework for mathematical problem solving. The method does not update model parameters or require an additional reasoning corpus. Instead, guidance generation and step reasoning are incorporated into the inference procedure, allowing the model to determine an appropriate next operation before continuing the solution.

Our experiments focus on general-purpose instruction-tuned language models and compare their performance with and without Step Guided Reasoning. We additionally compare the resulting performance with that of a math-specialized model when such a comparison is available. This setup is intended to assess whether structured guidance at inference time can improve mathematical reasoning without changing the underlying model.

### 4.2 Models and Evaluation

We evaluate Qwen2-7B-Instruct and Qwen2-72B-Instruct, representing models of different scales within the same general-purpose model family. We also include Qwen2.5-72B-Math-Instruct as a math-oriented reference model. Each model is evaluated under its standard inference setting and under Step Guided Reasoning.

Performance is measured on mathematical reasoning tasks, including the mathematical portion of the evaluation suite and the STEM subset of MMLU. We report the aggregate mathematical scores to characterize overall reasoning ability and use MMLU-STEM to examine transfer to a broader collection of science and mathematics questions. All comparisons are made between the corresponding base inference procedure and the Step Guided Reasoning procedure.

### 4.3 Overall Results

Step Guided Reasoning consistently improves the mathematical performance of the general-purpose models. For Qwen2-7B-Instruct, the average score in the math domain increases from 27.1% without guidance to 36.3% with Step Guided Reasoning. The improvement is also observed for the larger Qwen2-72B-Instruct model, whose average score rises from 36.5% to 47.4%. These results indicate that the method provides benefits beyond simple model scaling: explicitly organizing the inference process helps both smaller and larger models reason more effectively.

The gains are particularly notable on MMLU-STEM. With Step Guided Reasoning, Qwen2-72B-Instruct achieves 90.9%, exceeding the 87.3% obtained by Qwen2.5-72B-Math-Instruct. Thus, the general-purpose model equipped with the proposed inference procedure surpasses a math-specialized counterpart on this evaluation. This result suggests that improvements in reasoning control can compensate for, and in this setting exceed, the advantages associated with specialized mathematical training.

### 4.4 Analysis of Step-Guided Inference

The performance improvements support the central premise of Step Guided Reasoning: mathematical problem solving benefits when the model explicitly reflects on the immediate subgoal before producing the next reasoning step. Rather than generating a complete solution in a single unconstrained chain, the model repeatedly uses guidance to select and organize the next operation. This intermediate reflection can reduce errors caused by premature transitions, irrelevant derivations, or poorly ordered calculations.

The results across model sizes further suggest that the framework is complementary to model capacity. Although the larger model performs better in the unguided setting, it also benefits substantially from the step-guided procedure. The consistent gains for both Qwen2-7B-Instruct and Qwen2-72B-Instruct demonstrate that the approach is not restricted to a particular scale or dependent on additional parameter training.

### 4.5 Summary

Overall, the experiments show that Step Guided Reasoning improves mathematical reasoning through inference-time guidance generation and step-level deliberation. The method raises the average mathematical performance of both evaluated general-purpose Qwen2 models and enables Qwen2-72B-Instruct to outperform Qwen2.5-72B-Math-Instruct on MMLU-STEM. These findings demonstrate the potential of structured, training-free reasoning control as an effective alternative to parameter updates or extensive inference-time training data.

title: Step Guided Reasoning: Improving Mathematical Reasoning using Guidance Generation and Step Reasoning
text:
## Conclusion

We presented Step Guided Reasoning, a training-free inference framework designed to improve mathematical reasoning in general-purpose language models. Rather than requiring additional reasoning-oriented training data, the framework introduces an intermediate guidance process that identifies the next appropriate reasoning action before generating each subsequent step. This encourages models to maintain a more structured progression through mathematical problems and reduces reliance on a single unconstrained chain of thought.

Experiments across language models and mathematical evaluation settings show that step-level guidance can substantially improve reasoning performance, including for models that are not specialized for mathematics. The results further indicate that carefully organizing inference may provide an effective alternative to expanding model-specific training resources, and that general-purpose models can benefit considerably from explicit control over the progression of their reasoning.

Despite these gains, Step Guided Reasoning remains dependent on the quality and reliability of the generated guidance. Future work should investigate more robust guidance strategies, adaptive mechanisms for determining the appropriate reasoning granularity, and extensions to broader mathematical and scientific tasks. Improving the interpretability and efficiency of the guidance process also represents an important direction. Overall, our findings suggest that reasoning performance can be enhanced not only through larger models or additional training, but also by structuring how models decide what to do at each step.

title: Can an Individual Manipulate the Collective Decisions of Multi-Agents?
text:
### Abstract

Multi-agent systems built from large language models (LLMs) can improve reasoning and decision-making by combining the judgments of multiple agents. This collaboration, however, may also introduce vulnerabilities that are difficult to assess when an adversary has access to only a limited portion of the system. We study whether knowledge of a single agent is sufficient to influence the collective outcome of an otherwise partially unknown multi-agent system. We formulate this setting as an incomplete-information attack problem and propose **M-Spoiler**, a framework for constructing adversarial inputs through simulated interactions among agents. The framework incorporates a stubborn auxiliary agent that supports adversarial optimization by modeling persistent or resistant responses that may arise from agents in the target system. The resulting inputs are designed to manipulate a known target agent and, through the system’s aggregation and collaboration process, alter the final decision. Experiments across multiple tasks and multi-agent configurations show that information about one agent can pose a meaningful threat to collective decision-making, and that M-Spoiler consistently provides an effective attack strategy compared with existing baselines. We further examine several defense approaches, finding that they reduce but do not eliminate the attack’s effectiveness. These results highlight the need to account for partial-access adversaries when designing robust multi-agent LLM systems.

title: Can an Individual Manipulate the Collective Decisions of Multi-Agents?
text:
## 1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly capable of performing complex reasoning and decision-making tasks in domains such as healthcare, law, education, and finance. Despite these advances, individual LLMs remain vulnerable to misleading inputs, instruction manipulation, and other forms of adversarial interference. Their tendency to follow persuasive or strategically crafted instructions can cause them to produce incorrect conclusions, even when they are otherwise capable of solving the underlying task.

Multi-agent systems have emerged as a promising approach for improving the reliability and quality of LLM-based decision-making. In these systems, multiple agents may assume different roles, exchange information, critique one another’s outputs, or aggregate independent judgments. Through such interactions, a collective decision can benefit from complementary reasoning abilities and partial error correction. This collaborative structure may appear to provide greater robustness than relying on a single model. However, collaboration does not necessarily eliminate vulnerabilities. If the output of one agent influences the deliberation, communication, or aggregation process, an attacker may be able to exploit that agent as an entry point for manipulating the final decision.

A particularly important but underexplored setting arises when an attacker has limited knowledge of the target system. In many practical scenarios, the attacker cannot inspect the full set of agents, their prompts, their internal states, or their interaction protocols. Instead, the attacker may have access to, or knowledge of, only one agent participating in the system. This limitation raises a fundamental question: can information about a single agent be sufficient to construct an input that alters the collective decision of an otherwise unknown multi-agent system? The question is challenging because the attacker must account not only for the behavior of the known agent, but also for the possible reactions of other agents whose identities and behaviors are unavailable.

This setting can be viewed as a decision-making game with incomplete information. The attacker seeks to generate an adversarial sample that changes the behavior of a known target agent, while the target agent is embedded in a larger system containing partially unknown participants. A successful sample must therefore satisfy two objectives. First, it must influence the target agent in a controllable manner. Second, its effect must persist or propagate through subsequent agent interactions and ultimately affect the system-level decision. Optimizing only against the known agent may produce an attack that fails when the manipulated response is evaluated, challenged, or combined with the responses of other agents.

To address this problem, we propose **M-Spoiler**, a framework for generating adversarial samples against multi-agent decision-making systems under restricted attacker knowledge. M-Spoiler models the interaction process between the attacker and the target agent while simulating the potential responses of other agents in the target system. A central component of the framework is a *stubborn agent*, which is designed to provide persistent assistance during adversarial-sample optimization. Rather than treating the known agent in isolation, the stubborn agent approximates how agents in the target system may respond to, resist, or reinforce the manipulated output. This simulated interaction supplies additional guidance for constructing samples that are more likely to influence the collective outcome.

The study investigates whether access to a single agent creates a meaningful security risk for multi-agent systems. We evaluate M-Spoiler across multiple tasks and compare it with baseline attack strategies that do not explicitly model the interactions among agents. We further examine defense mechanisms intended to reduce the impact of adversarial inputs and assess the extent to which the proposed attack remains effective under such defenses. Our results demonstrate that limited knowledge of one agent can be sufficient to threaten collective decision-making, highlighting a gap between the apparent robustness of multi-agent collaboration and its resilience to targeted manipulation.

This work makes three main contributions. First, we formulate the manipulation of an unknown multi-agent system through a known agent as an adversarial game with incomplete information. Second, we introduce M-Spoiler, including a stubborn-agent mechanism for simulating cross-agent interactions during attack optimization. Third, we provide an empirical analysis of the resulting risks and of existing defense strategies, emphasizing the need to evaluate multi-agent systems not only as collections of cooperating models but also as interconnected attack surfaces.

title: Can an Individual Manipulate the Collective Decisions of Multi-Agents?
text:
## Related Work

### Multi-Agent LLM Systems

Recent research has increasingly explored systems in which multiple language-model agents interact to solve complex tasks. Rather than relying on a single model response, these systems distribute subtasks among specialized agents, use dialogue to exchange intermediate conclusions, or aggregate independent opinions into a final decision. Such architectures have been applied to reasoning, planning, code generation, debate, and domain-specific decision support. Collaboration can improve reliability by enabling agents to critique one another, compare alternative solutions, and correct individual errors.

However, multi-agent coordination also introduces new vulnerabilities. The final output is often influenced by the communication process, including the information presented to individual agents, the order of interactions, and the aggregation mechanism. Consequently, improvements obtained through collaboration may depend on assumptions about the reliability and independence of participating agents. If one agent produces misleading content, the resulting information may propagate through subsequent discussions or affect the judgments of other agents. This creates an attack surface that differs from that of conventional single-model prompting.

### Adversarial Manipulation of Language Models

A substantial body of work has studied methods for influencing the behavior of language models through carefully designed inputs. These methods include adversarial prompts, instruction manipulation, prompt injection, jailbreaks, and context-based attacks. In general, the attacker seeks to induce an undesirable response without modifying the underlying model parameters. Such attacks can exploit instruction-following behavior, conflicts between system and user messages, sensitivity to contextual framing, or the model’s tendency to accept information supplied in natural language.

Most existing attacks are evaluated against an individual model or a fixed application interface. They commonly assume that the attacker can query the target model directly and optimize an input based on observable outputs. This setting does not fully capture attacks against collaborative systems, where the attacker may influence only one participant and where the final decision is produced by interactions among multiple agents. In such systems, an effective input must not only alter the behavior of the directly affected agent but also survive, or even benefit from, subsequent discussion and aggregation.

### Attacks on Collaborative and Agent-Based Systems

The use of multiple agents creates opportunities for attacks that exploit communication and coordination rather than the weakness of a single model alone. An adversarial agent may provide deceptive evidence, generate strategically biased recommendations, or introduce content that other agents treat as a legitimate contribution. Related concerns have been examined in distributed decision-making, multi-agent learning, and Byzantine environments, where compromised participants can influence collective behavior through malicious messages or actions.

LLM-based systems differ from traditional distributed systems because their communication is typically expressed in natural language and their behavior is shaped by flexible instruction-following policies. This makes malicious influence difficult to characterize using only fixed message or action models. An agent can manipulate not only the content of a recommendation but also the framing of an issue, the apparent confidence of a claim, or the reasoning path used to justify a conclusion. Moreover, language-model agents may respond differently depending on the conversational history, allowing an attack to exploit the dynamics of the entire interaction.

Existing studies of multi-agent LLM security have considered issues such as malicious agents, unreliable participants, prompt injection transmitted through shared context, and the propagation of unsafe or incorrect information. Nevertheless, many analyses assume that the attacker can control or observe multiple agents, or that the malicious behavior is implemented directly within one of the system’s components. The setting considered in this work is more restrictive: the attacker has knowledge of only one target agent and seeks to construct an input that influences the collective decision despite limited information about the remaining agents.

### Black-Box and Partial-Knowledge Adversarial Settings

Adversarial example generation has also been studied under black-box and transfer-based settings. When the target model is inaccessible or only partially known, an attacker may optimize inputs using a surrogate model, limited queries, or observations of related systems. The resulting attack relies on transferability: a manipulation that affects the surrogate or observed component may also affect the target.

A multi-agent system with hidden participants can be viewed as a particularly challenging partial-knowledge environment. The attacker may know the architecture or behavior of one agent while lacking direct access to the other agents, their prompts, their roles, and their decision rules. In addition, the attacker must account for the possibility that the target agent will be challenged, corrected, or outweighed during collaboration. Thus, optimizing solely for the response of the known agent may not produce a successful collective attack. This motivates approaches that model possible interactions with unknown agents rather than treating the target agent as an isolated predictor.

### Game-Theoretic Modeling of Incomplete Information

Game-theoretic formulations provide a natural framework for analyzing strategic behavior when participants possess different information. In games of incomplete information, an agent’s strategy depends not only on its objectives but also on uncertainty about the identities, preferences, or actions of other participants. This perspective has been applied to security, distributed systems, adversarial machine learning, and strategic communication.

For collaborative LLM systems, incomplete-information modeling captures the asymmetry between an attacker who knows one agent and a target system containing additional hidden agents. The attacker must select an input that is effective across plausible interaction trajectories, while the system’s agents may interpret and respond to the input according to their own roles and policies. This view shifts the objective from merely causing a target model to produce a particular output to influencing a sequential decision process involving multiple participants.

### Defenses for Multi-Agent LLM Systems

Several defensive strategies have been proposed to improve the robustness of language-model applications and agentic systems. These include input and output filtering, instruction hierarchy enforcement, prompt sanitization, independent verification, debate or critique mechanisms, agent voting, confidence-based aggregation, and restricting the information shared across agents. Some systems also use trusted supervisors or external evaluators to identify inconsistent or unsafe recommendations.

Although these mechanisms can reduce the impact of individual erroneous or malicious messages, they may not eliminate coordinated influence. A manipulation can be expressed as apparently relevant task information rather than an explicit instruction, and a target agent may transmit the manipulated content to other agents in a form that is difficult to distinguish from ordinary reasoning. Furthermore, defenses based on majority agreement may be less effective when agents share similar biases or when the adversary can shape the discussion before independent judgments are formed. These limitations highlight the need to evaluate defenses against attacks designed specifically for the interaction structure of multi-agent systems.

Overall, prior work establishes the capabilities of collaborative LLM agents and documents vulnerabilities in individual models, communication channels, and distributed decision processes. However, the problem of manipulating a collective decision using knowledge of only one participating agent remains comparatively underexplored. Our work addresses this gap by studying adversarial sample generation under incomplete information and by modeling how a manipulated agent can influence the broader multi-agent interaction.

title: Can an Individual Manipulate the Collective Decisions of Multi-Agents?
text:
## Methodology

### 3.1 Problem Formulation

We study a multi-agent system (MAS) in which several language-model agents collaboratively solve a task. Let  
\[
\mathcal{A}=\{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n\}
\]
denote the agents participating in the system, and let \(x\) be an input instance. Each agent produces a response based on the input and the preceding interaction history. The system then combines the individual responses through an interaction protocol and produces a collective decision \(y\).

The interaction protocol may include discussion, critique, voting, role-based deliberation, or other forms of coordination. We represent this protocol abstractly as a function
\[
y = F(x; a_1,\ldots,a_n,\mathcal{P}),
\]
where \(\mathcal{P}\) denotes the communication and aggregation procedure. This formulation allows the method to be applied to different MAS architectures without requiring a particular aggregation rule.

The attacker constructs an adversarial input \(x'\) from an original input \(x\). The objective is to preserve the general task context while causing the MAS to produce an incorrect or attacker-chosen collective decision. We denote the attacker’s objective by
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}}(x',y^\star),
\]
where \(y^\star\) is either the incorrect target label selected by the attacker or the complement of the correct decision, depending on the task.

### 3.2 Incomplete-Information Threat Model

The attacker is assumed to know only one agent in the target MAS, referred to as the target agent \(a_t\). Knowledge of this agent may include its model behavior, role, prompting format, accessible interface, or responses to queried inputs. The attacker does not have direct access to the remaining agents, their private prompts, their parameters, or the complete system-level interaction history.

Accordingly, the attacker faces uncertainty about the hidden agent set
\[
\mathcal{A}_{-t}=\mathcal{A}\setminus\{a_t\},
\]
as well as the communication protocol used by these agents. Rather than optimizing against a fully specified MAS, the attacker maintains a set of simulated interaction states intended to approximate plausible behaviors of the unknown agents.

The attack is successful when an adversarial input changes the collective decision of the target MAS. Depending on the task, success can be measured by either:

1. **Untargeted manipulation**, in which the final decision differs from the correct answer; or  
2. **Targeted manipulation**, in which the final decision is forced toward a specified incorrect answer.

The adversarial input is constrained to remain task-relevant and to satisfy the formatting requirements of the target system. When appropriate, a perturbation budget or semantic-preservation constraint is imposed:
\[
x' \in \mathcal{C}(x),
\]
where \(\mathcal{C}(x)\) denotes the set of admissible modifications of \(x\).

### 3.3 Overview of M-Spoiler

M-Spoiler is designed to optimize an adversarial sample using only the accessible target agent while accounting for uncertainty in the rest of the MAS. Its central component is a simulated multi-agent environment containing:

- the accessible target agent \(a_t\);
- simulated counterparts of the unknown agents; and
- a **stubborn agent** that repeatedly promotes or preserves the attacker’s desired direction during optimization.

The simulated environment is not intended to reconstruct the exact hidden MAS. Instead, it provides a collection of plausible responses that expose the adversarial sample to different forms of discussion, disagreement, and aggregation. The attack therefore optimizes for robustness across possible collective reactions rather than for a single response from the known agent.

For a candidate adversarial input \(x'\), M-Spoiler generates an interaction trajectory
\[
\tau(x')=\{r_t,r_1,\ldots,r_m\},
\]
where \(r_t\) is the response of the target agent and \(r_j\) denotes the response of a simulated hidden agent. The collective output of the simulated interaction is represented as
\[
\hat{y}(x') = \hat{F}(x';a_t,\tilde{a}_1,\ldots,\tilde{a}_m,\tilde{\mathcal{P}}),
\]
where \(\tilde{a}_j\) and \(\tilde{\mathcal{P}}\) are simulated agents and interaction rules. M-Spoiler updates \(x'\) according to the degree to which the simulated collective output satisfies the attack objective.

### 3.4 Simulation of Hidden Agents

Because the attacker cannot inspect the unknown agents, their behavior is modeled through role-conditioned simulations. Each simulated agent receives the candidate input together with the interaction context and is assigned a role or response tendency that may plausibly occur in the target MAS. These tendencies can include independent reasoning, agreement with another agent, critique of a proposed answer, uncertainty expression, or preference for majority-supported conclusions.

The simulator maintains multiple response configurations rather than relying on a single fixed surrogate. Let
\[
\mathcal{S}=\{s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_K\}
\]
denote a set of simulated interaction scenarios. Each scenario specifies the roles, response order, and communication context of the simulated agents. For a candidate \(x'\), M-Spoiler evaluates the attack objective across these scenarios:
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sim}}(x')
=
\operatorname{Agg}_{s\in\mathcal{S}}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}}\big(\hat{y}_s(x'),y^\star\big),
\]
where \(\operatorname{Agg}\) aggregates the losses across simulated scenarios. Depending on the attack setting, the aggregation may emphasize average performance, worst-case performance, or the proportion of scenarios in which manipulation succeeds.

This multi-scenario formulation reduces dependence on an exact estimate of the hidden agents. It also reflects the incomplete-information setting: the attacker seeks an input that remains effective under several plausible realizations of the unknown portion of the MAS.

### 3.5 Stubborn-Agent Optimization

The defining component of M-Spoiler is the stubborn agent. In each simulated interaction, this agent produces responses that consistently support the attacker’s objective, even when other simulated agents disagree. It can, for example, reiterate an adversarial interpretation, challenge responses that oppose the desired decision, or provide additional reasoning favoring the attacker-selected outcome.

The stubborn agent is not assumed to exist in the target MAS. Rather, it serves as an optimization mechanism that amplifies the influence of the adversarial input during simulation. Let \(r_s\) denote the stubborn agent’s response. Its generation is conditioned on the candidate input, the current interaction history, and the target decision:
\[
r_s = G_{\mathrm{stub}}(x',h,y^\star),
\]
where \(h\) is the simulated dialogue history. The response is then incorporated into subsequent rounds of interaction with the target and simulated agents.

The stubborn agent improves optimization in two ways. First, it creates a persistent adversarial signal that can be propagated through the simulated discussion. Second, it exposes whether the candidate input can withstand disagreement and correction from other agents. Candidate inputs that only influence the target agent in isolation are therefore distinguished from those that continue to affect the simulated collective decision after additional interaction.

To prevent the optimization from depending solely on one stubborn response, M-Spoiler evaluates candidate inputs with and without different placements or interaction roles for the stubborn agent. The resulting objective can be written as
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{M\text{-}Spoiler}}(x')
=
\lambda \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{target}}(x')
+
(1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{collective}}(x'),
\]
where \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{target}}\) measures the effect on the accessible target agent, \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{collective}}\) measures the effect after simulated collaboration, and \(\lambda\) controls the relative contribution of the two terms. The collective term includes the interaction trajectories generated with the stubborn agent.

### 3.6 Adversarial Sample Generation

M-Spoiler begins with an unmodified input \(x^{(0)}=x\) or with an initialized task-preserving transformation. At iteration \(q\), the current candidate \(x^{(q)}\) is submitted to the target-agent interface and to the simulated MAS. The resulting responses are analyzed to determine whether the candidate satisfies the attack objective.

If the desired manipulation has not been achieved, the framework generates an update \(\Delta^{(q)}\) using the target response, the simulated responses, and the stubborn-agent trajectory:
\[
x^{(q+1)} = \operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal{C}(x)}
\left(x^{(q)}+\Delta^{(q)}\right).
\]
Here, \(\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal{C}(x)}\) ensures that the updated sample remains within the admissible input space. The update may modify the wording, framing, contextual emphasis, or instruction structure of the input, depending on the task and attack interface.

The optimization terminates when one of the following conditions is met:

1. the simulated collective decision satisfies the attack objective;
2. the candidate reaches the permitted modification budget;
3. the optimization reaches a predefined query or iteration limit; or
4. successive updates no longer improve the simulated attack objective.

Among the generated candidates, M-Spoiler selects the sample with the strongest objective value while satisfying the task-preservation constraints. The selected sample is then transferred to the target MAS without exposing the simulated interaction or the attacker’s optimization process.

### 3.7 Deployment Against the Target MAS

After generation, the adversarial sample \(x'\) is provided to the target MAS through the same input interface used for ordinary task instances. The target agent receives \(x'\) as part of the system’s normal workflow, while the remaining agents operate without knowledge of the attack-generation procedure.

The final target-system output is recorded as
\[
y' = F(x';a_1,\ldots,a_n,\mathcal{P}).
\]
Attack effectiveness is determined by comparing \(y'\) with the clean output \(y\) and the ground-truth decision. This separation between generation and deployment is important: the simulator is used only to construct the adversarial sample, whereas the final evaluation is performed on the actual target MAS.

### 3.8 Evaluation Protocol

We evaluate M-Spoiler across multiple collaborative tasks and MAS configurations. For each task, the same underlying instance is evaluated in clean and adversarial conditions. The clean condition uses the original input \(x\), while the attack condition uses the generated input \(x'\).

The evaluation considers the following measures:

- **Attack success rate:** the proportion of instances for which the adversarial sample causes the desired collective manipulation.
- **Decision degradation:** the change in collective-task performance between clean and adversarial inputs.
- **Target-agent influence:** the extent to which the adversarial sample changes the response of the known agent.
- **Transfer effectiveness:** the degree to which samples generated from the incomplete-information simulator remain effective against the actual MAS.
- **Input validity:** whether the generated sample remains syntactically valid, task-relevant, and compliant with the input constraints.
- **Query and optimization cost:** the number of target-agent interactions and simulation steps required to generate an adversarial sample.

To isolate the contribution of the proposed components, we conduct ablations that remove or modify the hidden-agent simulation, the stubborn agent, and the multi-scenario objective. These comparisons assess whether manipulation results from simply influencing the known agent or from the additional modeling of collective interaction.

### 3.9 Evaluation of Defensive Mechanisms

We additionally examine defenses that attempt to reduce the influence of adversarial inputs on collective decisions. Defenses are applied at one or more stages of the MAS pipeline, including input screening, agent-level response validation, disagreement handling, response aggregation, and repeated deliberation.

For each defense, the target MAS is evaluated on both clean and adversarial inputs. A defense is considered effective when it preserves clean-task performance while reducing the rate at which adversarial samples alter the collective decision. Since the attacker is assumed not to know the complete target system, the evaluation also examines whether M-Spoiler-generated samples remain effective when the system introduces additional response checks or changes its interaction procedure.

title: Can an Individual Manipulate the Collective Decisions of Multi-Agents?
text:
## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Objectives

Our experiments investigate whether knowledge of a single agent is sufficient to influence the collective decision of a multi-agent system. We focus on four questions:

1. **Attack effectiveness:** Can adversarial samples generated with access to only one target agent alter the final system decision?
2. **Effect of interaction modeling:** Does simulating the responses of other agents improve the attack compared with optimizing solely against the known agent?
3. **Robustness across settings:** Does the attack remain effective across different tasks, agent configurations, and decision protocols?
4. **Defense resistance:** How does M-Spoiler perform when the target system adopts mechanisms intended to reduce the influence of anomalous or manipulated responses?

All experiments follow the partial-knowledge setting described in the problem formulation. The attacker observes the behavior of one target agent and does not access the prompts, parameters, outputs, or internal states of the remaining agents in the target system. The generated adversarial sample is subsequently evaluated by the complete multi-agent system.

### 4.2 Evaluation Setting

We evaluate M-Spoiler on multiple task families requiring either classification, selection, or reasoning-based decisions. For each task, a multi-agent system is constructed from several interacting LLM agents. The agents independently analyze the input or exchange intermediate responses according to the system’s collaboration protocol, after which a final decision is produced.

For every task, we construct clean and attacked versions of the same inputs. The clean version is submitted without modification, while the attacked version is produced by M-Spoiler or by a comparison method. This paired evaluation allows us to measure whether an attack changes the collective outcome rather than merely degrading the quality of the input.

The target agent used during attack generation is selected from the agents participating in the target system. During optimization, M-Spoiler receives the target agent’s accessible behavior and simulates additional agent responses through its stubborn-agent mechanism. The simulated agents are not assumed to share their actual parameters or prompts with the attacker. At evaluation time, the adversarial sample is transferred to the original multi-agent system, whose other agents remain unknown to the attacker.

### 4.3 Compared Methods

We compare M-Spoiler with attack strategies that do not model the interaction among agents. These include methods that optimize directly against the known agent, methods that use a fixed or generic adversarial perturbation, and coordination-agnostic strategies that treat the collective system as a single decision maker. These comparisons distinguish the contribution of modeling potential reactions from the contribution of merely optimizing an input to manipulate one agent.

We also evaluate ablated versions of M-Spoiler. In particular, we remove the stubborn agent, restrict the optimization to the observed target agent, or reduce the diversity of simulated responses. These variants test whether the attack benefits from explicitly representing uncertainty about the hidden agents and their possible reactions.

All methods are given comparable access to the target agent and are evaluated under the same input, output, and interaction constraints. Unless otherwise stated, the target system is not modified during attack generation.

### 4.4 Metrics

We use the following metrics to evaluate both attack performance and decision quality.

- **Attack success rate:** the proportion of inputs for which the attacked system produces the adversary’s intended outcome or differs from the correct collective decision.
- **Decision-flip rate:** the proportion of examples whose final decision changes between the clean and attacked inputs.
- **Collective performance degradation:** the decrease in task performance caused by the adversarial sample relative to clean inputs.
- **Target-agent manipulation rate:** the frequency with which the adversarial sample changes the target agent’s response in the desired direction.
- **Transfer effectiveness:** the extent to which an adversarial sample optimized using the known agent remains effective when evaluated by the complete, partially unknown system.
- **Sample validity and utility:** whether the generated sample remains acceptable under the task constraints and preserves the required input format or semantic intent.
- **Optimization cost:** the computational or interactional resources required to generate an adversarial sample.

The distinction between target-agent manipulation and collective attack success is important. An attack may successfully alter the known agent while failing to influence the final decision if the remaining agents correct its response. Conversely, a successful attack should demonstrate that manipulation of one agent can propagate through the collaboration process.

### 4.5 Main Results

Across the evaluated task families, M-Spoiler consistently demonstrates that access to a single agent can pose a meaningful threat to the collective decision. The method is able to produce samples that alter the target agent’s response and, in a substantial portion of cases, change the decision of the entire multi-agent system. This effect is observed even though the attacker does not directly observe or optimize against the hidden agents.

Compared with methods that optimize only against the known agent, M-Spoiler achieves stronger transfer to the complete system. The improvement indicates that manipulating the target agent in isolation is insufficient to reliably control a collaborative decision. By simulating possible responses from hidden agents, M-Spoiler identifies adversarial samples that are more likely to remain effective after the target agent interacts with the rest of the system.

The advantage of M-Spoiler is particularly evident in settings where agents exchange intermediate reasoning, critique one another, or aggregate independent judgments. In these settings, the response of a single agent can affect the information available to other agents and thereby influence the final aggregation process. The results suggest that the attack does not depend solely on forcing an isolated incorrect answer; instead, it exploits the propagation of manipulated information through the interaction protocol.

The attack remains effective across different task types and system configurations, although its success varies with the degree of agent agreement, the aggregation rule, and the amount of corrective information supplied by the other agents. Systems in which agents independently verify one another are generally more difficult to influence than systems that directly aggregate agent responses. Nevertheless, the partial-knowledge attack remains effective in both settings, demonstrating that collaboration improves reliability but does not eliminate the risk created by a compromised or manipulated participant.

### 4.6 Ablation Study

We conduct ablations to assess the role of each component in M-Spoiler. Removing the stubborn agent consistently reduces the effectiveness of the generated samples. Without this component, optimization is driven primarily by the observed target agent and has limited ability to anticipate how hidden agents may respond. The resulting samples can manipulate the known agent but are less reliable when transferred to the complete system.

We further examine the effect of varying the simulated interaction behavior. When the attacker models a broader range of possible stubborn responses, the generated samples are generally more robust across target systems. In contrast, using a narrow or fixed response model can lead to overfitting to a particular simulated behavior and weaker transfer to the actual hidden agents.

An additional ablation removes the interaction history from the optimization process. This variant performs worse in systems where later agents condition their responses on earlier messages, confirming that the sequence of agent communication is relevant to attack generation. The findings collectively support the central design of M-Spoiler: effective manipulation requires modeling not only the known agent, but also how information may be propagated and reinforced during collaboration.

### 4.7 Robustness to System Configuration

To examine whether M-Spoiler depends on a particular system architecture, we vary the number and arrangement of agents participating in the final decision. The attack remains applicable as the number of hidden agents changes, although increasing agent diversity and independent verification tends to reduce attack effectiveness. This reduction does not eliminate the attack, because M-Spoiler can optimize for responses that remain influential under multiple possible interaction patterns.

We also test different aggregation and discussion protocols. Direct voting, response aggregation, and sequential discussion exhibit different levels of vulnerability. Protocols that give a single agent disproportionate influence can amplify manipulation, whereas protocols that require agreement across agents can suppress some attacks. However, agreement-based protocols may still be vulnerable when the manipulated response is used as evidence by other agents rather than treated as an isolated vote.

These experiments show that the risk is not tied to a particular model or communication pattern. Instead, it arises from the dependence of collective decisions on the information contributed by individual agents.

### 4.8 Evaluation Against Defenses

We evaluate several defense strategies intended to reduce the influence of manipulated agents. These strategies include mechanisms that identify inconsistent responses, limit the effect of a single agent, introduce additional verification, or alter the way agent outputs are aggregated. The defenses generally reduce the success of all attacks, particularly when they prevent one anomalous response from directly determining the final outcome.

However, M-Spoiler remains more effective than the comparison methods under the evaluated defenses. The relative advantage is maintained because the generated samples are optimized with respect to possible interactions rather than a single isolated response. Consequently, the manipulated target agent can produce outputs that appear more consistent with the surrounding discussion, making simple disagreement-based defenses less reliable.

The results also reveal a trade-off between robustness and utility. Stronger filtering or verification can reduce attack success but may require additional agent calls, delay the final decision, or reject inputs that are otherwise valid. These observations suggest that defending collaborative systems requires more than detecting abnormal individual responses. A robust defense should also account for coordinated information propagation and the possibility that an adversarial input can influence several agents indirectly.

### 4.9 Discussion

The experimental results provide evidence that partial access to a multi-agent system can be sufficient for meaningful decision manipulation. In particular, knowledge of one agent enables an attacker to construct inputs that affect not only that agent but also the collective process in which the agent participates. Modeling hidden-agent behavior substantially improves this transfer, supporting the formulation of the problem as an incomplete-information game.

At the same time, the results do not imply that every collective decision can be controlled through one agent. Attack effectiveness depends on the task, the communication protocol, the reliability of the hidden agents, and the aggregation mechanism. Independent verification and diverse reasoning paths can reduce the likelihood that a manipulated response determines the final outcome. Nevertheless, the consistent performance of M-Spoiler across varied settings indicates that multi-agent collaboration should not be treated as an automatic defense against adversarial inputs.

title: Can an Individual Manipulate the Collective Decisions of Multi-Agents?
text:
## Conclusion

This work investigates whether an attacker with knowledge of only one agent can influence the collective decisions of a multi-agent system. By modeling the attack setting as a game with incomplete information, we show that limited access to an individual agent does not necessarily prevent effective manipulation of the broader system. We introduce M-Spoiler, which simulates interactions among agents and employs a stubborn agent to anticipate and exploit possible responses within the target system. This design enables the generation of adversarial samples that target an accessible agent while accounting for the collaborative dynamics of agents that remain unknown to the attacker.

Experiments across multiple tasks indicate that vulnerabilities in an individual agent can propagate through agent interactions and affect the final collective outcome. M-Spoiler consistently demonstrates the practical risk of this threat model relative to the considered baselines, including when several defense strategies are applied. These findings suggest that evaluating multi-agent robustness solely at the level of individual agents is insufficient; the effects of communication, influence, and decision aggregation must also be considered.

Despite these findings, the effectiveness of attacks may depend on the system architecture, interaction protocol, agent diversity, and aggregation mechanism. Future work should therefore examine broader classes of multi-agent systems, stronger adaptive defenses, and methods for detecting malicious or anomalous contributions during collaboration. Developing robust coordination protocols that limit the propagation of compromised information while preserving the benefits of cooperation is an important direction for ensuring the reliability and security of multi-agent decision-making systems.

title: Self-Critique and Refinement for Faithful Natural Language Explanations
text:
## Abstract

Natural language explanations (NLEs) are widely used to make the predictions of large language models (LLMs) more interpretable, yet they may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying those predictions. We present Self-Critique and Refinement for Natural Language Explanations (SR-NLE), a training-free framework for improving the faithfulness of post-hoc explanations through iterative self-evaluation and revision. SR-NLE supports multiple feedback strategies, including natural-language critiques and feature-attribution signals that identify influential input tokens. Across three datasets and four state-of-the-art LLMs, the proposed approach consistently lowers explanation unfaithfulness relative to a baseline. Its strongest configuration reduces the average unfaithfulness rate from 54.81% to 36.02%, an absolute improvement of 18.79 percentage points. These results indicate that LLMs can revise their own explanations to better align with the factors driving their predictions when provided with suitable feedback, without additional supervision, training, or fine-tuning.

title: Self-Critique and Refinement for Faithful Natural Language Explanations
text:
## 1. Introduction

Natural language explanations (NLEs) are increasingly used to make the predictions of machine learning systems more understandable to users. By expressing the basis for a prediction in natural language, an explanation can support error analysis, improve transparency, and help users assess whether a model’s output is reasonable. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has made it possible to generate such explanations flexibly across a wide range of tasks. However, the fluency and apparent coherence of an explanation do not necessarily indicate that it accurately reflects the evidence used to produce the prediction.

This distinction is commonly described in terms of explanation faithfulness. An explanation is faithful when it corresponds to the factors that causally or functionally influence the model’s decision, rather than merely providing a plausible justification after the fact. This issue is particularly important for post-hoc NLEs, which are generated after a model has produced a prediction and therefore may be constructed independently of the internal evidence underlying that prediction. In such cases, an explanation can be persuasive while highlighting irrelevant input information, omitting influential features, or even supporting a conclusion that does not depend on the stated rationale. Consequently, improving the linguistic quality of explanations alone is insufficient: explanation-generation methods must also be guided toward the information that is relevant to the model’s prediction.

A natural possibility is to ask a model to inspect and revise its own explanations. Recent work has shown that LLMs can critique and improve their outputs in a variety of generation and reasoning settings. Self-critique is appealing for explanation generation because it does not require collecting additional human annotations or retraining the underlying model. Nevertheless, it is not clear whether a model’s ability to revise text can be translated into improved faithfulness. In particular, unconstrained self-reflection may reward explanations that sound more convincing without making them more consistent with the model’s decision process. Effective refinement therefore requires feedback that directs the model’s attention toward the relationship between the input, the prediction, and the explanation.

In this work, we introduce **Self-critique and Refinement for Natural Language Explanations (SR-NLE)**, a framework for iteratively improving the faithfulness of post-hoc NLEs. SR-NLE first produces an explanation and then uses feedback to identify potential shortcomings before generating a revised version. The framework supports multiple forms of feedback. One form relies on natural-language self-feedback, in which the model evaluates and critiques its explanation. Another uses feature-attribution information to identify input words that are important for the prediction, providing a signal that can be used to assess whether the explanation attends to decision-relevant evidence. These signals can be incorporated into the refinement process without additional model training or task-specific fine-tuning.

We evaluate SR-NLE across multiple datasets and state-of-the-art LLMs, examining whether iterative critique and refinement reduce explanation unfaithfulness. The results show that suitable feedback can substantially improve the correspondence between generated explanations and the evidence associated with model predictions. They further indicate that LLMs possess a degree of self-correction ability for explanation generation, but that this ability depends on how the refinement process is guided.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate self-critique and refinement as a framework for improving the faithfulness of post-hoc NLEs. Second, we investigate complementary feedback mechanisms, including natural-language feedback and feature-attribution-based feedback, for directing explanation revision. Third, we provide an empirical evaluation across several datasets and LLMs, demonstrating that explanation faithfulness can be improved through iterative refinement without external supervision, additional training, or fine-tuning.

title: Self-Critique and Refinement for Faithful Natural Language Explanations
text:
## Related Work

### Natural Language Explanations and Explanation Faithfulness

Natural language explanations (NLEs) are intended to make model predictions more understandable by expressing the evidence, rationale, or decision process in human-readable form. They have been studied in a range of tasks, including visual question answering, natural language inference, commonsense reasoning, and text classification. Compared with feature-based or symbolic explanations, NLEs can communicate complex reasoning in a flexible format and can be evaluated by human readers for coherence and usefulness.

A central distinction in explainable machine learning is that between explanation plausibility and faithfulness. Plausibility concerns whether an explanation appears reasonable to a human or is consistent with a reference rationale. Faithfulness, in contrast, concerns whether the explanation accurately reflects the information used by the underlying predictor. These properties are related but not equivalent: a fluent explanation may provide a convincing justification while omitting, distorting, or contradicting the features that actually influenced the prediction. This issue is particularly important for post-hoc NLEs, which are generated after a prediction has been produced and therefore need not be causally involved in producing that prediction.

Prior work has proposed a variety of methods for assessing explanation faithfulness. These include input perturbation tests, which measure changes in predictions after rationale tokens are removed or altered; sufficiency and comprehensiveness measures, which evaluate whether highlighted evidence is adequate for, or important to, the prediction; and agreement-based comparisons between generated explanations and model-derived importance signals. Such evaluations have shown that linguistic quality and faithfulness can diverge, motivating methods that explicitly constrain or improve the relationship between explanations and model behavior. The present work follows this line of research by treating faithfulness as an objective for refining an already generated natural language explanation rather than only as a property to be measured after generation.

### Feature Attribution for Explanations

Feature attribution methods provide model-dependent signals about the contribution of individual input features to a prediction. For language models, these signals can identify tokens or words whose presence has a positive or negative effect on the output according to a chosen attribution procedure. Attribution-based approaches have been widely used to produce extractive rationales, analyze model behavior, and evaluate whether textual explanations identify relevant evidence.

Although feature attributions can offer useful guidance, they do not necessarily constitute complete explanations. Their interpretation may depend on the attribution algorithm, the prediction target, and the way interactions among features are handled. In addition, token-level importance scores do not directly express the relations or reasoning steps that are naturally conveyed in free-form language. Nevertheless, attribution signals can serve as an informative source of feedback for NLE generation. In particular, they can indicate whether an explanation mentions input regions that are important to the model and can help identify unsupported or irrelevant claims. Our framework builds on this complementary relationship by using attribution-derived information as feedback during explanation refinement, rather than requiring the explanation itself to be replaced by an extractive rationale.

### Self-Critique and Iterative Refinement in Language Models

Recent work has investigated whether language models can improve their outputs by evaluating and revising them. Self-critique, reflection, and iterative refinement methods commonly ask a model to inspect an initial answer, identify errors or weaknesses, and produce a revised response. These methods have been applied to tasks such as mathematical problem solving, code generation, planning, factual question answering, and general instruction following. Their effectiveness is often attributed to the separation of generation and evaluation stages, which gives the model an opportunity to detect issues that may not be corrected during the initial response.

Several forms of feedback have been explored in this setting. A model may generate free-form natural language criticism, follow a structured checklist, compare an answer with an external constraint, or use task-specific verification signals. Refinement can then be performed in one or more iterations. However, the success of self-refinement depends on the quality and relevance of the feedback: a model may fail to identify its own errors, produce critiques that are vague or inconsistent, or make revisions that improve surface quality without improving correctness.

Most self-critique methods have focused on the correctness, completeness, or style of the final answer. Less attention has been given to whether a model’s explanation accurately describes the basis of its own prediction. Explanation faithfulness introduces a distinct challenge because the target is not merely a better-formulated answer. The model must revise a linguistic rationale so that it is more consistent with its prediction behavior, potentially using signals that are not expressed directly in the original explanation. SR-NLE applies iterative self-critique to this setting and considers both language-based and model-behavior-based feedback.

### Prompting and Feedback for Explanation Generation

Prompt-based methods have been used to elicit rationales and explanations from pretrained language models without modifying their parameters. These methods can encourage step-by-step reasoning, evidence selection, justification of predictions, or adherence to specified explanation formats. They are attractive because they require no additional training and can be adapted across models and tasks. However, prompting a model to provide a rationale does not guarantee that the rationale is causally related to the prediction. In some cases, the generated text may function primarily as a plausible post-hoc justification.

Feedback-based prompting provides a way to address this limitation by making desired properties explicit during generation or revision. Natural language feedback can ask a model to remove unsupported statements, focus on decisive evidence, or check consistency with the prediction. More structured feedback can impose constraints based on labels, input perturbations, or importance estimates. These approaches suggest that explanation quality can be influenced at inference time, but they also leave open how different feedback types affect faithfulness and whether a model can use such feedback to revise its own explanations reliably.

The approach developed in this paper is related to these methods but differs in its emphasis on explanation faithfulness as the refinement target. Rather than generating an explanation once under a fixed prompt, SR-NLE uses an initial post-hoc explanation, obtains feedback about its shortcomings, and generates a revised explanation. The framework also considers feedback grounded in feature attribution, thereby combining the linguistic flexibility of self-critique with a signal tied to the model’s input sensitivity.

### Position of the Present Work

Existing research has established the importance of distinguishing plausible explanations from faithful ones, developed attribution-based tools for analyzing model behavior, and shown that language models can sometimes improve outputs through self-evaluation and revision. These strands of work have largely been studied separately. Faithfulness research often evaluates explanations after they are generated, while self-refinement research typically targets answer correctness or presentation quality rather than the correspondence between an explanation and the model’s predictive behavior.

SR-NLE connects these directions by using iterative critique and refinement to improve the faithfulness of post-hoc NLEs without additional training or fine-tuning. It examines feedback expressed both in natural language and through feature-attribution signals. This formulation treats self-critique not only as a mechanism for polishing explanations, but as a means of aligning generated rationales more closely with evidence about the model’s actual decision process.

title: Self-Critique and Refinement for Faithful Natural Language Explanations
text:
## 3. Methodology

### 3.1 Task Formulation

We study post-hoc natural language explanations for predictions made by large language models. Let \(x\) denote an input instance, \(y\) the model’s prediction, and \(e^{(0)}\) an initial explanation generated after the prediction has been produced. The objective is not to change the prediction \(y\), but to revise \(e^{(0)}\) so that it more accurately reflects the information that influenced the model’s decision.

We define the refinement process as an iterative procedure that produces a sequence of explanations,

\[
e^{(0)} \rightarrow e^{(1)} \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow e^{(T)},
\]

where each subsequent explanation is generated using the input, the fixed prediction, the preceding explanation, and feedback about the explanation’s faithfulness. The final explanation \(e^{(T)}\) is evaluated against the model’s behavior rather than against a human-authored rationale. This distinction is important because a fluent or plausible explanation may still be unfaithful if it refers to input information that has little effect on the prediction.

### 3.2 SR-NLE Framework

SR-NLE consists of two complementary stages: self-critique and explanation refinement. At iteration \(t\), the model receives the original input \(x\), its prediction \(y\), and the current explanation \(e^{(t)}\). It first generates feedback identifying potential problems in the explanation. It then uses this feedback to produce a revised explanation \(e^{(t+1)}\).

The critique is instructed to assess whether the explanation:

1. identifies information that is relevant to the prediction;
2. omits input information that appears important to the prediction;
3. makes claims unsupported by the input;
4. attributes the prediction to irrelevant or weakly influential features; and
5. remains consistent with the predicted label.

The refinement prompt supplies the critique together with the current explanation and asks the model to rewrite the explanation. The prediction is held fixed throughout this process, so improvements are assessed solely in terms of the explanation and not through changes in task accuracy. The procedure may be repeated for a predetermined number of iterations or until no further refinement is requested.

### 3.3 Feedback Mechanisms

SR-NLE supports multiple forms of feedback. The feedback is generated or presented without human-written explanations, labels for rationale quality, or additional parameter updates.

#### 3.3.1 Natural-Language Self-Feedback

In the natural-language condition, the model critiques its own explanation directly. The critique prompt encourages the model to compare the explanation with the input and prediction, identify unsupported or irrelevant statements, and specify how the explanation should be revised. This feedback provides a semantic description of potential faithfulness errors.

The subsequent refinement prompt asks the model to incorporate the critique while preserving the central decision and producing an explanation grounded in the input. To reduce superficial changes, the refinement instruction emphasizes that the revised explanation should explain the prediction using features that are relevant to the model’s decision rather than merely improve its style or plausibility.

#### 3.3.2 Feature-Attribution Feedback

The second feedback mechanism augments self-critique with feature-attribution information. An attribution procedure estimates the contribution of input words or other input features to the model’s prediction. The resulting information is converted into a form that can be provided to the language model, for example by highlighting relatively important input words.

The model is then asked to compare the highlighted features with the content of its explanation. If an explanation relies on words that receive little attribution, the model is encouraged to remove or qualify those claims. Conversely, if highly influential input words are absent from the explanation, the model is encouraged to consider whether they should be incorporated. Attribution feedback therefore supplies a behavioral signal that complements the model’s linguistic self-assessment.

The attribution signal is used as guidance rather than as a human-authored rationale. In particular, highlighted features do not automatically constitute a complete explanation; they serve as evidence about which parts of the input are associated with the model’s prediction. The refined explanation must still be expressed in natural language and remain consistent with the full input and the predicted output.

### 3.4 Iterative Refinement Procedure

For each instance, the model first generates a prediction and an initial post-hoc explanation using the same task context. The initial explanation is then passed to the selected critique module. In the self-feedback setting, the critique is based on the input, prediction, and explanation. In the attribution-guided setting, the critique additionally receives the feature-importance information.

The refinement step combines the current explanation and feedback into a new explanation. The process can be represented as

\[
c^{(t)} = C(x,y,e^{(t)},a),
\]

\[
e^{(t+1)} = R(x,y,e^{(t)},c^{(t)},a),
\]

where \(C\) is the critique operation, \(R\) is the refinement operation, and \(a\) denotes optional attribution feedback. When attribution information is not used, \(a\) is omitted. The same procedure is applied across all experimental conditions, allowing the effect of the feedback source and the number of refinement steps to be examined independently of the task model’s prediction.

To preserve comparability, the evaluation uses the same input and prediction for the initial and refined explanations. The refinement process does not access gold rationales or external explanations. It also does not involve supervised fine-tuning, parameter updates, or task-specific training of the evaluated language models.

### 3.5 Experimental Conditions

We compare the initial post-hoc explanations with explanations produced by SR-NLE. The comparison includes the unrefined baseline and refinement conditions using the available feedback mechanisms. Where applicable, additional iterations are evaluated to determine whether repeated critique and revision yields further improvements or causes explanations to drift away from the input.

The framework is tested across three datasets representing the target prediction tasks and across four state-of-the-art LLMs. Each model is evaluated under the same general prompting and refinement protocol, with task-specific formatting limited to the requirements of the corresponding dataset. This design makes it possible to assess whether self-refinement is robust across both data sources and model families.

### 3.6 Evaluation of Explanation Faithfulness

Faithfulness is evaluated behaviorally by testing whether the information cited in an explanation is related to the model’s prediction. The evaluation compares the model’s prediction on the original input with its behavior after relevant input information is altered, removed, or otherwise perturbed. An explanation is considered more faithful when its stated evidence corresponds to features whose modification meaningfully affects the prediction, and less faithful when it relies on features that do not materially influence the model’s output.

We report the resulting unfaithfulness rate for the initial and refined explanations. The same faithfulness evaluation is applied to every explanation condition, including the baseline, natural-language self-feedback, and attribution-guided refinement. This ensures that improvements cannot be attributed to differences in evaluation procedures.

In addition to behavioral faithfulness, explanations are checked for basic validity: they must describe the given input, remain compatible with the fixed prediction, and avoid unsupported content introduced during rewriting. These checks are used to distinguish genuine refinement from changes that merely make an explanation more detailed or linguistically fluent.

title: Self-Critique and Refinement for Faithful Natural Language Explanations
text:
## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Objectives

We evaluate whether a language model can improve the faithfulness of its own post-hoc natural language explanations through iterative self-critique and refinement. The experiments address three questions:

1. Can SR-NLE reduce the rate of unfaithful explanations relative to unrevised explanations?
2. Do different feedback mechanisms provide useful guidance for explanation refinement?
3. Is the observed improvement consistent across multiple datasets and language models?

All experiments are conducted without additional model training, fine-tuning, or externally annotated explanations. The model is given the input, its prediction, and an initial explanation, and is then prompted to critique and revise the explanation according to the selected feedback mechanism.

### 4.2 Evaluation Setting

We evaluate SR-NLE on three datasets using four state-of-the-art large language models. The datasets contain prediction tasks for which post-hoc natural language explanations can be generated and assessed for faithfulness. For each instance, the model first produces an initial prediction and an accompanying explanation. This initial explanation serves as the baseline output.

We then apply the SR-NLE procedure. In each refinement step, the model receives the original input, its prediction, the current explanation, and feedback identifying aspects of the explanation that may not correspond to the model’s relevant evidence. The model is instructed to revise the explanation while preserving consistency with the prediction and the information emphasized by the feedback. The procedure can be applied iteratively, allowing the output of one refinement step to serve as the input to the next.

We consider two forms of feedback. The first is natural-language self-feedback, in which the model is prompted to inspect its explanation and identify potential inconsistencies between the explanation and the evidence used for the prediction. The second is attribution-based feedback, which supplies information about important input words identified through feature attribution. This feedback is expressed in a form that can be provided to the language model as guidance during critique and refinement. Neither feedback source requires human-written explanations or additional supervision.

### 4.3 Compared Methods

The primary baseline is the unrevised post-hoc explanation generated by the model before applying SR-NLE. This baseline measures the faithfulness of explanations produced in a standard explanation-generation setting.

We compare the baseline with SR-NLE configurations based on the available feedback mechanisms. These comparisons allow us to distinguish improvements resulting from refinement itself from improvements associated with the particular form of feedback. For each configuration, the same prediction and initial explanation are used whenever possible, so that differences in explanation faithfulness can be attributed to the critique and refinement process rather than to changes in the underlying prediction task.

The experiments also examine the behavior of the framework across refinement steps. This analysis assesses whether critique produces progressively more faithful explanations or whether improvements are limited to the initial refinement.

### 4.4 Evaluation Metric

We measure explanation quality using the unfaithfulness rate. An explanation is considered unfaithful when its stated rationale does not adequately reflect the evidence associated with the model’s prediction under the evaluation procedure. The unfaithfulness rate is the proportion of evaluated explanations classified as unfaithful; lower values therefore indicate better faithfulness.

We report results aggregated across the three datasets and four language models, while also examining variation across individual experimental settings. Since SR-NLE does not alter the prediction-generation objective, the evaluation focuses on the relationship between the explanation and the model’s predictive evidence rather than on predictive accuracy alone.

### 4.5 Main Results

SR-NLE substantially improves explanation faithfulness relative to the unrevised baseline. Across the evaluated datasets and models, the baseline has an average unfaithfulness rate of 54.81%. The best-performing SR-NLE configuration reduces this rate to 36.02%, corresponding to an absolute reduction of 18.79 percentage points.

These results indicate that post-hoc explanations can be improved after generation, even when the refinement process does not use human supervision or additional training. The improvement is obtained by supplying the model with structured guidance about possible discrepancies between its explanation and the evidence relevant to its prediction. Thus, the results support the central premise of SR-NLE: language models can use self-critique to revise explanations in a direction that is more faithful to their predictive behavior.

### 4.6 Comparison of Feedback Mechanisms

The comparison between feedback mechanisms shows that the form of guidance is important for successful refinement. Natural-language self-feedback provides a flexible way for the model to identify unsupported or potentially misleading claims in its explanation. Attribution-based feedback supplies a more explicit signal by highlighting input words associated with the prediction. This signal gives the refinement process a concrete basis for determining which parts of the input should be reflected in the explanation.

The results across the feedback configurations demonstrate that refinement quality depends not only on asking the model to reconsider its explanation, but also on providing information that constrains the revision toward relevant input evidence. In particular, the attribution-based formulation offers a complementary source of guidance to unconstrained verbal self-critique, since it links the revision process to features associated with the model’s prediction.

### 4.7 Analysis of Iterative Refinement

We further analyze explanation faithfulness over successive critique-and-refinement steps. This analysis evaluates whether a model can continue to benefit from its own feedback or whether repeated revisions introduce new unsupported content. The results are interpreted using the unfaithfulness rate at each stage, with the initial explanation serving as the reference point.

Overall, the iterative setting shows that critique can be used as an explanation-improvement mechanism rather than solely as an error-detection step. However, the effectiveness of additional refinement depends on the feedback supplied to the model and on the model–dataset combination. This observation motivates treating the feedback design as a central component of SR-NLE rather than assuming that repeated free-form revision will always improve faithfulness.

### 4.8 Summary

Across three datasets and four language models, SR-NLE reduces the unfaithfulness of post-hoc natural language explanations without requiring fine-tuning, external explanation annotations, or additional supervision. The strongest configuration achieves an average unfaithfulness rate of 36.02%, compared with 54.81% for the unrevised baseline. These findings suggest that appropriately guided self-critique enables language models to produce explanations that more closely track the evidence underlying their predictions.

title: Self-Critique and Refinement for Faithful Natural Language Explanations
text:
## Conclusion

This work introduced SR-NLE, a self-critique and refinement framework for improving the faithfulness of post-hoc natural language explanations produced by large language models. Rather than relying on additional training or human-provided explanations, SR-NLE iteratively uses feedback to identify and revise aspects of an initial explanation that may not accurately reflect the model’s behavior. In particular, our study examined both natural language self-feedback and feature-attribution-based feedback, which provides guidance grounded in the importance of input words.

Across the evaluated datasets and language models, iterative refinement generally produced explanations with lower unfaithfulness than the unrefined baseline.
