These results suggest that LLMs possess a degree of capacity to assess and revise their own explanations, but that this capacity is more effective when the self-critique process is provided with suitable signals about the model’s decision-relevant features. The findings therefore highlight feedback design as an important factor in developing more faithful explanation-generation methods.

At the same time, SR-NLE does not eliminate the broader challenges associated with evaluating and generating faithful natural language explanations. Its effectiveness may depend on the quality of the attribution signal, the formulation of the critique prompt, and the number of refinement steps. Future work should investigate more robust feedback mechanisms, assess the framework on a wider range of tasks and model architectures, and develop evaluation procedures that better capture the relationship between explanations and underlying model behavior. More generally, self-critique and refinement offer a promising direction for improving explanation faithfulness without modifying the underlying model.

title: L iterary QA : Towards Effective Evaluation of Long-document Narrative QA
text:
**Abstract.**  
Long-document question answering over narrative texts requires models to integrate information across extended and structurally complex contexts. Progress in this setting is difficult to assess reliably because the widely used NarrativeQA benchmark contains both noisy source documents and imperfect question–answer pairs. We present LiteraryQA, a curated subset centered on literary works, developed through a validation pipeline combining human review with large language model assistance. The resulting resource improves question–answer quality and removes irrelevant material from the associated documents. We further conduct a meta-evaluation of automatic assessment methods, examining their agreement with human judgments at the system level. Our findings indicate that conventional n-gram metrics provide weak evidence for system ranking, whereas LLM-based judges—including relatively small open-weight models—more closely reproduce human preferences. Finally, we evaluate several long-context language models on LiteraryQA, establishing a benchmark for future research in narrative question answering. The data, evaluation tools, and code are available at https://github.com/sapienzaNLP/LiteraryQA.

title: L iterary QA : Towards Effective Evaluation of Long-document Narrative QA
text:
## 1 Introduction

Answering questions about literary narratives requires more than locating a passage that contains a matching phrase. A system must track entities and events across long stretches of text, resolve references, identify information that is distributed across multiple scenes, and distinguish central developments from incidental details. These demands make narrative question answering (QA) a particularly challenging setting for evaluating language understanding over long documents. They also expose limitations in standard QA methodologies, which often assume relatively short contexts and questions whose answers can be verified through local textual evidence.

NarrativeQA is one of the principal resources for studying this problem. Its documents include literary works and other long-form narratives, while its questions are designed to test understanding of events and plot-level information. Despite its importance, the benchmark presents difficulties for reliable system comparison. The source documents may contain material that is not relevant to the questions, and the associated question–answer pairs can vary in clarity, factual grounding, and answer quality. Such noise affects both model training and evaluation: systems may be penalized for producing valid answers that differ from imperfect references, while automatic metrics may reward superficial lexical overlap rather than faithful understanding of the narrative.

These issues are especially consequential when evaluating recent long-context language models. As models become increasingly capable of processing extended inputs, differences in their performance may be smaller and more sensitive to evaluation artifacts. A benchmark that does not adequately control document relevance and answer quality can therefore obscure meaningful progress. Moreover, the metrics commonly used for generative QA are not necessarily suitable for open-ended narrative answers. Overlap-based measures provide a convenient and reproducible protocol, but they can undervalue paraphrases and fail to assess whether an answer captures the essential content of a response. Establishing an evaluation methodology that better reflects human judgments is thus an essential complement to improving the underlying models.

In this work, we introduce **LiteraryQA**, a curated subset of NarrativeQA centered on literary works. Our goal is to provide a cleaner and more dependable setting for studying long-document narrative QA without changing the fundamental nature of the task. We construct the resource through a quality-control pipeline that combines human assessment with validation by large language models. This process identifies problematic question–answer instances, corrects issues where possible, and removes portions of source documents that are extraneous to the benchmarked task. The resulting collection is intended to reduce avoidable noise while preserving the long-range reasoning challenges characteristic of narrative understanding.

We further investigate how generated answers should be evaluated on this resource. Specifically, we conduct a meta-evaluation of automatic metrics by comparing their system-level behavior with human assessments. The analysis considers both conventional n-gram-based measures and judge-based evaluations performed by language models. Our findings indicate that lexical-overlap metrics provide a weak basis for ranking systems in this setting, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge approaches can more closely reproduce human preferences, including when using relatively small open-weight models. These results suggest that evaluation design, rather than only model architecture or context length, plays a central role in determining what progress on narrative QA is observed.

Finally, we use LiteraryQA to benchmark a collection of long-context language models. This benchmark provides an empirical comparison under the curated data and evaluation protocols developed in this work, and illustrates the practical value of separating data quality from metric quality. In summary, our contributions are:

1. We introduce LiteraryQA, a quality-controlled literary subset of NarrativeQA designed for long-document narrative question answering.
2. We develop a human- and LLM-assisted procedure for detecting and repairing unreliable QA instances and filtering irrelevant document content.
3. We assess automatic evaluation methods against human judgments, highlighting the limitations of n-gram overlap and the potential of LLM-based judging.
4. We benchmark long-context language models on the resulting resource and release the data and code to support future research.

Through these contributions, LiteraryQA aims to facilitate more reliable measurement of progress in narrative QA and to support the development of systems that can reason over extended literary documents.

title: L iterary QA : Towards Effective Evaluation of Long-document Narrative QA
text:
## Related Work

### Narrative Question Answering

Question answering over narrative text differs from conventional reading comprehension in both scale and reasoning requirements. Answers may depend on information distributed across chapters, indirect references, character motivations, and events whose significance emerges only through the broader plot. Consequently, narrative QA often requires abstraction and synthesis rather than the extraction of a contiguous answer span.

NarrativeQA (Kočiský et al., 2018) established a widely used benchmark for this setting. It contains questions about books and movie scripts, together with answers written in natural language, and includes both full documents and shorter summaries. The benchmark has consequently supported research on long-document reading, hierarchical encoding, retrieval, and abstractive answer generation. Subsequent work has explored methods for selecting relevant passages, representing documents at multiple levels of granularity, and combining local evidence with global narrative structure. However, the benchmark also illustrates a recurring difficulty in evaluating narrative QA: documents can contain substantial irrelevant material, while questions and reference answers may vary in specificity, completeness, and faithfulness to the source.

Other datasets have broadened the study of long-form narrative and document understanding. BookSum (Kryściński et al., 2021), for example, focuses on summarization of books and other long works, and therefore emphasizes the modeling of discourse structure over extended contexts. QuALITY (Pang et al., 2022) evaluates comprehension of long documents through difficult multiple-choice questions, while more recent long-context benchmarks, such as LongBench (Bai et al., 2023), cover a range of tasks involving lengthy inputs. These resources are valuable for assessing context handling and long-range reasoning, but they do not fully address the evaluation of free-form answers to literary questions. LiteraryQA is positioned within this setting by concentrating on narrative QA instances in literary works and by examining the quality of both the underlying data and the evaluation process.

### Evaluation of Generated Answers

Automatic evaluation for question answering has traditionally relied on lexical-overlap measures. BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) compares candidate and reference answers using matching n-grams, whereas ROUGE (Lin, 2004) emphasizes recall-oriented overlap and is frequently used for summarization. METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005) incorporates stemming and synonym matching, and embedding-based metrics such as BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020) compare contextual representations rather than exact word sequences. These measures are convenient, inexpensive, and reproducible, but their assumptions are particularly restrictive for narrative QA. A valid answer may use different wording from the reference, provide a justified paraphrase, or organize several pieces of evidence in a different way. Conversely, substantial lexical overlap does not guarantee that an answer is correct, complete, or appropriately grounded in the document.

The limitations of surface-form metrics have motivated human evaluation and task-specific assessment protocols. Human judgments can account for dimensions such as factual correctness, relevance, completeness, and coherence, but they are costly and may be difficult to reproduce at scale. In addition, agreement among evaluators can be affected by underspecified questions and by the fact that narrative questions often admit multiple acceptable formulations. These considerations make benchmark curation and metric validation closely connected: unreliable questions or references can obscure the extent to which an automatic metric reflects genuine answer quality.

Recent work has investigated the use of language models as evaluators. Frameworks such as G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023) and studies of pairwise evaluation in MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023) demonstrate that capable language models can assess open-ended generations using natural-language criteria. LLM-based judges can evaluate semantic equivalence and discourse-level adequacy more flexibly than n-gram metrics. At the same time, they may be sensitive to answer position, verbosity, stylistic preferences, prompt design, and the characteristics of the model used for judging. Their judgments therefore require calibration against human assessments rather than being treated as inherently reliable. The evaluation of smaller open-weight models as judges is especially relevant when reproducibility, cost, and access are important considerations.

### Data Quality and Long-Context Evaluation

Data quality is a central concern in benchmarks for complex language understanding. Annotation errors, ambiguous questions, incomplete references, and noisy source documents can introduce an upper bound on apparent system performance and make comparisons between models difficult. In long-document settings, the problem is amplified because documents may contain metadata, duplicated material, formatting artifacts, or sections unrelated to the question. A system can therefore be penalized for failing to process irrelevant text, while a model may also exploit unintended cues that are unrelated to narrative understanding.

Research on long-context language models has largely focused on increasing context-window capacity, improving information retrieval within long inputs, and testing whether models can use evidence that appears at different positions in a document. Benchmarks such as LongBench provide broad evaluations of long-context capabilities, while work on retrieval augmentation and hierarchical processing addresses the practical difficulty of reasoning over documents that exceed the effective attention span of a model. Nevertheless, context length alone is not a sufficient measure of narrative comprehension. Literary QA additionally requires resolving references, integrating events across distant passages, and distinguishing central evidence from narratively incidental detail.

LiteraryQA contributes to this line of work by treating benchmark construction and evaluation as joint methodological concerns. Rather than considering the original dataset as fixed, it applies validation and correction procedures to question-answer instances and removes extraneous material from the source documents. It further examines the extent to which commonly used automatic metrics reproduce human preferences and uses this analysis to inform the comparison of long-context language models. In this way, the benchmark is intended not only to test model capabilities, but also to provide a more reliable basis for interpreting results in long-document narrative question answering.

title: L iterary QA : Towards Effective Evaluation of Long-document Narrative QA
text:
## Methodology

### 3.1 Dataset Construction

We construct LiteraryQA from the literary portion of NarrativeQA. The objective is to preserve the original task—answering questions about long narrative documents—while reducing noise in both the documents and the associated question–answer pairs. The resulting dataset retains the original narrative setting and evaluation format, but applies quality-control procedures to the textual inputs and annotations.

For each example, we associate a question with its corresponding literary document and reference answer. We inspect the document boundaries to identify material that is unrelated to the narrative being queried, such as metadata, platform-specific descriptions, duplicated content, or other text introduced during document collection. This extraneous material is removed while preserving the narrative content required for answering the question. The procedure is applied consistently across the corpus and is designed to avoid altering the events, entities, and discourse structure relevant to the task.

### 3.2 Question–Answer Quality Control

Quality control is performed at the level of individual question–answer instances. Candidate examples are examined for properties that can make evaluation unreliable, including ambiguity, insufficient evidence in the associated document, incorrect or incomplete reference answers, mismatches between questions and answers, and questions that depend on information outside the supplied narrative. Examples that cannot be made reliable through revision are excluded.

For examples that remain suitable for inclusion, annotators revise the question or reference answer when necessary. Revisions are constrained by the source document: a question must be answerable from the document, and the reference answer must accurately reflect the information supported by the narrative. The goal is not to simplify the underlying reasoning problem, but to ensure that the benchmark measures a model’s ability to understand the document rather than its ability to handle annotation artifacts.

The curation process combines human review with language-model-assisted validation. Human annotators make or verify the final decisions concerning document relevance, question validity, and answer correctness. Language models are used as an additional quality-control component to identify potentially problematic instances and to support consistency checks. Their judgments are treated as signals for review rather than as an unconditional replacement for human annotation. Disagreements and uncertain cases are resolved through further inspection, with preference given to evidence available in the source narrative.

### 3.3 Evaluation Protocol

We evaluate generated answers against the curated reference answers using both lexical and model-based approaches. Lexical evaluation includes n-gram-overlap metrics, which compare the surface form of a prediction with one or more references. These metrics provide a reproducible baseline, but they may penalize valid paraphrases and may reward superficial word overlap. We therefore supplement them with an LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation.

For model-based evaluation, a judge model receives the question, the relevant narrative context, the reference answer, and a candidate answer according to a fixed prompt and scoring procedure. The judge assesses whether the candidate provides an adequate answer to the question and whether it is supported by the document. The evaluation protocol is kept constant across systems, including the prompt structure, response format, and decision rule, so that model comparisons are based on the same criteria. We examine judges with different model capacities, including smaller open-weight models, to assess whether reliable evaluation requires a large proprietary evaluator.

### 3.4 Meta-Evaluation of Automatic Metrics

To determine how well automatic metrics reflect human preferences, we conduct a meta-evaluation over system outputs on LiteraryQA. Human assessment supplies the reference ordering of systems. We then compare this ordering with the rankings induced by each automatic metric.

The analysis is conducted at the system level: scores are aggregated over the evaluation examples for each system, and the resulting metric-based rankings are compared with the human ranking using an appropriate rank-correlation analysis. This setup evaluates whether a metric can distinguish stronger and weaker QA systems, rather than only whether it assigns similar scores to individual answers. We analyze lexical metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge configurations under the same set of system outputs and compare their agreement with human judgments. The evaluation also considers the effect of the judge model used, allowing us to assess the robustness of model-based judging across evaluator sizes and model families without conflating changes in the judge with changes in the QA systems.

### 3.5 Long-Context Model Benchmark

We benchmark long-context language models on the LiteraryQA documents using a common question-answering protocol. Each model receives the question together with the associated narrative document, without document-specific retrieval annotations or manually selected evidence passages. This setting tests the ability to locate and integrate information distributed throughout a long literary work.

For each model, generation settings and input formatting are held fixed as far as supported by the model interface. The model produces a free-form answer to each question, and the resulting outputs are evaluated using the automatic metrics considered in the meta-evaluation. We additionally apply the selected LLM-as-a-Judge procedure to enable comparison under a semantically oriented evaluation criterion. All systems are assessed on the same curated examples and document versions, ensuring that differences in performance are attributable to the models rather than to variation in the underlying data or preprocessing.

The released implementation contains the data-processing procedures, evaluation scripts, and benchmarking code required to reproduce the curation and evaluation pipeline.

title: L iterary QA : Towards Effective Evaluation of Long-document Narrative QA
text:
## 4. Experiments

We evaluate LiteraryQA from two complementary perspectives. First, we assess the reliability of automatic evaluation metrics by comparing their judgments with human assessments. Second, we use the resulting evaluation protocol to benchmark long-context language models on narrative question answering. Our experiments are designed to address the following questions:

1. How does the quality of the evaluation material affect the assessment of narrative QA systems?
2. Do conventional lexical metrics provide a reliable estimate of answer quality on literary texts?
3. Can language-model-based judges reproduce human preferences between system outputs?
4. How well do current long-context language models perform on LiteraryQA?

### 4.1 Experimental Data

All experiments use the LiteraryQA collection introduced in this work. The collection consists of question–answer pairs grounded in literary documents, together with source texts from which extraneous material has been removed. We use the corrected questions and answers produced by the annotation and validation pipeline, rather than the corresponding unfiltered instances from NarrativeQA.

For each question, a system receives the associated document and is asked to produce a free-form answer. The document is provided in its entirety whenever the model context permits it; otherwise, we follow the context-handling procedure supported by the evaluated model. This setting reflects the intended use of LiteraryQA: answering questions that require integrating information distributed across a long narrative rather than retrieving a short supporting span.

We preserve the original dataset partitioning for evaluation and avoid using test answers during model prompting or metric calibration. Human judgments and metric analyses are conducted on system outputs generated for the same set of questions, allowing the different evaluators to be compared under identical conditions.

### 4.2 Evaluation Metrics

We compare several families of automatic metrics. The first family consists of surface-form metrics based on lexical overlap between a generated answer and the reference answer. These metrics include standard n-gram precision, recall, or harmonic-overlap measures, as well as related variants commonly used for free-form QA evaluation. They provide a useful baseline because they are inexpensive and deterministic, but they may be sensitive to paraphrasing, answer length, and differences in wording.

The second family consists of evaluations performed by a language model acting as a judge. Given a question, the relevant document, a reference answer, and a system answer, the judge is instructed to assess whether the system answer is correct and sufficiently supported by the narrative. We use both closed- or hosted-model settings when available and smaller open-weight models to examine whether strong agreement with humans requires a large proprietary evaluator. The judging prompt is kept consistent across systems, and model outputs are converted into comparable scores for aggregation.

For all metrics, we compute scores at the question level and aggregate them to obtain a system-level performance estimate. Since narrative answers can be expressed in multiple valid ways, the main focus of the meta-evaluation is system ranking rather than exact agreement on individual examples.

### 4.3 Human Evaluation and Meta-Evaluation

We construct a human preference signal by asking annotators to compare system answers with respect to their correctness and adequacy for the question. Annotators are instructed to consider the information conveyed by an answer rather than its lexical similarity to the reference. In particular, an answer is favored when it captures the relevant events, entities, relations, or interpretations supported by the source narrative, even if its wording differs from the reference. Answers that contain unsupported claims or omit essential information are penalized.

The human judgments are aggregated into a ranking of the evaluated systems. We then measure how closely each automatic metric reproduces this ranking. The primary analysis is conducted at the system level, using rank correlation between automatic scores and the human ordering. We additionally inspect question-level judgments to identify common sources of disagreement, including valid paraphrases, partial answers, overly general responses, and answers that are fluent but inconsistent with the document.

This design separates two properties that are often conflated in QA evaluation: sensitivity to answer quality on individual examples and reliability when comparing complete systems. A metric may assign plausible scores to individual answers while still failing to distinguish stronger systems from weaker ones. We therefore use system-level agreement as the main criterion for selecting an evaluation method for LiteraryQA.

### 4.4 Long-Context QA Benchmark

We next evaluate a set of long-context language models on the LiteraryQA task. The models are prompted to answer each question using the associated literary document as context. We retain a common task formulation across models and vary only the model-specific requirements imposed by their interfaces, such as the maximum context length or decoding configuration. Generated answers are evaluated with the metrics examined in the meta-evaluation, with particular emphasis on the judge-based protocol that most closely tracks human preferences.

The benchmark includes models designed to process long inputs, covering different model families and parameter scales where possible. We do not interpret raw scores as a direct measure of general language ability: performance depends jointly on context handling, narrative comprehension, instruction following, and answer generation. We therefore report both aggregate performance and qualitative comparisons across the evaluated systems.

In addition to overall results, we examine how model behavior is affected by document length and by the type of reasoning required by the question. This analysis distinguishes questions that can be answered from a local passage from those requiring the integration of information across distant parts of the narrative. We also inspect representative errors, including missed evidence, incorrect entity resolution, confusion between events, and answers that introduce details not supported by the source.

### 4.5 Results Summary

The metric comparison shows that lexical-overlap measures are not reliable indicators of system quality in this setting. Their system rankings exhibit weak agreement with human preferences, reflecting the difficulty of evaluating narrative answers when correct responses may differ substantially in wording from the reference. This limitation is especially apparent for answers involving abstraction, temporal relations, or the combination of evidence from multiple parts of a document.

By contrast, language-model-based judging provides substantially stronger agreement with the human system ranking. This pattern is not limited to large evaluators: smaller open-weight judges can also reproduce human preferences when they are given the question, document, reference answer, and model output in a structured evaluation prompt. These findings motivate the use of judge-based evaluation as the primary measure for the LiteraryQA benchmark, while retaining lexical metrics as supplementary diagnostic measures.

The long-context benchmark further demonstrates that narrative QA remains challenging for current models. Strong performance requires more than accommodating a large input: models must locate relevant evidence, connect events and entities across the document, and produce an answer that is both complete and faithful to the narrative. The resulting benchmark therefore provides a demanding test bed for evaluating progress in long-document understanding and offers a more dependable basis for comparing future narrative QA systems.

title: L iterary QA : Towards Effective Evaluation of Long-document Narrative QA
text:
## Conclusion

We introduced LiteraryQA, a curated benchmark for evaluating question answering over long literary documents. By combining human review with LLM-assisted validation, our data construction process addresses both unreliable question–answer instances and irrelevant material in the source texts. This produces a more focused evaluation setting for studying narrative understanding in long documents.

Our meta-evaluation shows that commonly used n-gram-based metrics provide limited evidence about the relative quality of system outputs at the system level. In contrast, LLM-based judging offers substantially better alignment with human assessments, including when using smaller open-weight models. These findings suggest that evaluation methodology is a central concern for progress in long-document narrative QA, and that automatic metrics should be selected based on their agreement with human judgments rather than their convenience or widespread use.

Finally, we benchmarked long-context language models on LiteraryQA, establishing a reference point for future research on literary question answering. The benchmark and accompanying resources are intended to support more reliable comparisons among models and evaluation methods. Future work should expand the coverage of literary genres and languages, further examine the robustness and biases of LLM-based evaluators, and develop evaluation procedures that better capture the multifaceted nature of narrative understanding.

title: Large Language Models Discriminate Against Speakers of G erman Dialects
text:
## Abstract

Regional dialects are central to linguistic and cultural identity, yet their speakers are often subject to unfavorable social evaluations. This study investigates whether large language models (LLMs) reproduce such evaluations for speakers of German dialects. Drawing on sociolinguistic research on dialect perception, we examine two forms of bias: dialect naming bias, reflected in associations with dialect speakers, and dialect usage bias, reflected in responses to dialectal language. We evaluate both biases through an association task and a decision-making task. In addition, we introduce an evaluation corpus pairing sentences from seven German regional dialects, including Alemannic and Bavarian, with corresponding Standard German formulations. Across the evaluated models, dialect speakers receive predominantly negative adjective associations, and similar biases emerge in model decisions. The findings indicate that LLMs systematically reproduce negative stereotypes associated with German dialects. Moreover, explicitly identifying speakers as German dialect speakers intensifies these biases relative to presenting dialect use without an explicit demographic label, contrasting with findings from related work on other demographic categories.

title: Large Language Models Discriminate Against Speakers of G erman Dialects
text:
## Introduction

Language variation is a central feature of human communication and an important marker of social and regional identity. Dialects, in particular, convey information about speakers’ geographic origins, social affiliations, and cultural backgrounds. In Germany, regional varieties remain widely used: more than 40% of the population reportedly speaks a regional dialect (Adler and Hansen, 2022). Despite their cultural and communicative significance, German dialects have historically been evaluated through social hierarchies that privilege Standard German. Speakers of regional varieties may consequently be associated with unfavorable characteristics or be perceived as less competent, educated, or socially prestigious. Such evaluations can affect how dialect speakers are treated in education, employment, and everyday interaction.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have created new settings in which these social evaluations may be reproduced. LLMs are trained on large collections of human-generated text and can therefore reflect patterns of association present in their training data. Bias in these systems is not limited to explicit classifications or offensive language. It may also emerge in the traits attributed to social groups, in the decisions made about them, or in the way linguistic variation is interpreted. Because language itself can function as a cue to social identity, dialects offer an important case for examining whether LLMs reproduce language-based stereotypes.

Although research on bias in language technologies has examined demographic groups and varieties of English, the treatment of regional German dialects by LLMs remains comparatively underexplored. This gap is consequential for two reasons. First, dialect discrimination concerns not only the content of model outputs but also the evaluation of a legitimate form of linguistic diversity. Second, dialect-based cues provide an opportunity to distinguish between two related sources of bias. A model may express bias when a group is explicitly identified as dialect-speaking, which we refer to as dialect naming bias. Alternatively, it may infer or reproduce social evaluations from the use of dialectal language itself, which we refer to as dialect usage bias. Examining both forms is necessary to determine whether negative associations depend on an explicit demographic label or can also be elicited by linguistic form.

In this paper, we investigate these questions for seven regional German dialects, including Alemannic and Bavarian. We draw on sociolinguistic work concerning the traits conventionally associated with dialect speakers and use these traits to evaluate LLM behavior in two complementary settings. In an association task, we examine the adjectives that models connect with dialect speakers and with dialect use. In a decision task, we assess whether the same associations influence model judgments. To evaluate dialect usage bias systematically, we introduce a corpus that pairs sentences written in regional dialects with corresponding sentences in Standard German. This paired design allows us to compare responses to equivalent content while varying the linguistic variety.

Our study addresses three related questions. First, do LLMs associate German dialect speakers with the socially unfavorable traits documented in sociolinguistic research? Second, do these associations affect model decisions when dialect use or dialect identity is relevant? Third, does an explicit reference to the linguistic group produce a different level of bias than dialectal language used without such a label? By considering both explicit naming and implicit linguistic cues, we examine whether models reproduce dialect stereotypes through social descriptions, linguistic processing, or both.

The results show that the evaluated LLMs express negative associations with German dialect speakers in the association task and carry these biases into their decisions. They also indicate that explicitly identifying speakers as members of the relevant linguistic group can intensify bias relative to relying on dialect use as an implicit cue. These findings contribute to the study of language-based bias in LLMs and highlight the importance of evaluating linguistic diversity beyond standard-versus-nonstandard distinctions. More broadly, they demonstrate that dialect-sensitive evaluation is necessary for understanding how models represent speakers whose language differs from a socially dominant standard.

title: Large Language Models Discriminate Against Speakers of G erman Dialects
text:
## Related Work

### Social evaluation of dialects

Sociolinguistic research has long shown that dialects are evaluated not only as linguistic varieties but also as signals of social identity, regional belonging, and group membership. Although dialect use is often associated with solidarity and authenticity within local communities, speakers may also be judged through stereotypes concerning intelligence, competence, education, trustworthiness, or social status. These evaluations can vary according to the listener, the social context, and the perceived prestige of the dialect. Standard-language varieties are frequently treated as more appropriate in institutional and formal settings, while regional varieties may be framed as informal, less prestigious, or less suitable for professional communication. Work on German language attitudes similarly documents the coexistence of regional pride and negative judgments toward speakers of particular dialects. This literature motivates examining dialect bias as a multidimensional phenomenon rather than assuming that all regional varieties receive the same social evaluation.

A distinction central to the present study is that between attitudes toward dialect speakers and attitudes toward dialect forms. The former concerns the traits attributed to people who are identified as dialect speakers, whereas the latter concerns judgments made when dialectal language is encountered without an explicit speaker label. These dimensions need not coincide. A model may associate dialect speakers with negative characteristics when asked directly about the group, yet respond differently when evaluating a dialectal utterance in context. Separating these sources of bias makes it possible to investigate whether linguistic form itself functions as a social cue and whether explicit demographic framing changes model behavior.

### Bias in language models

Research on large language models has documented systematic associations between language and demographic or social attributes. Bias has been examined through tasks involving word associations, sentence completion, text generation, classification, and decisions about hypothetical individuals. Such studies show that models can reproduce patterns found in their training data, including stereotypes related to gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, age, and socioeconomic status. Importantly, model bias is not limited to overtly discriminatory statements. It may also appear through differences in sentiment, trait attribution, ranking, recommendation, or the selection of adjectives associated with a social group.

Existing evaluations commonly distinguish between explicit and implicit forms of demographic information. In an explicit condition, a group is directly named, whereas in an implicit condition, group membership must be inferred from linguistic, contextual, or cultural cues. Prior work suggests that models do not always behave identically across these conditions, and some studies report comparatively limited bias when demographic categories are explicitly mentioned. However, the effect of explicit linguistic-demographic labels may depend on the social category under investigation and on the task used to measure bias. German dialect speakers provide a useful case for this question because dialect can function simultaneously as a linguistic feature and as an index of regional identity.

### Dialect and language variation in NLP

Natural language processing has traditionally devoted greater attention to standardized language varieties than to regional and socially marked varieties. This imbalance affects both data availability and model evaluation. Dialectal language may be underrepresented in training resources, inconsistently transcribed, or treated as noisy deviation from a standard. Consequently, models may show reduced performance on dialectal input, even when the relevant issue is not linguistic comprehension alone but the social meaning attributed to the variety.

Recent work on multilinguality, language variation, and inclusive language technologies has emphasized that variation within a language can be as consequential as variation across languages. Studies of dialect-aware modeling have addressed tasks such as identification, speech recognition, translation, and text classification. These efforts primarily focus on technical performance, while fewer evaluations ask how models socially evaluate dialect speakers or how they make decisions when dialect is used as evidence about a person. An assessment of dialect bias therefore complements conventional robustness benchmarks by considering the social consequences of model outputs.

German offers a particularly relevant setting for this analysis. It contains numerous regional varieties that differ in phonology, vocabulary, morphology, and syntax, while Standard German remains dominant in education, administration, and much written communication. The relationship between regional speech and the standard is thus not adequately captured by a simple language-versus-language distinction. A meaningful evaluation must account for variation among dialects and should compare dialectal expressions with semantically corresponding standard-language forms. Such paired comparisons help isolate the contribution of dialectal realization from the content of the sentence.

### Evaluation of social bias in LLMs

Bias benchmarks for language models typically use controlled prompts, matched stimuli, or counterfactual substitutions to compare model behavior across social groups. Association-based methods measure the valence or stereotypical content of model-generated attributes, while decision-based methods examine choices made in scenarios involving employment, trust, competence, or other socially consequential judgments. Combining these approaches is useful because models may express bias in descriptive associations without necessarily making different decisions, or may make disparate decisions even when their verbal explanations appear neutral.

For dialects, both forms of evaluation are important. A naming condition can test whether models attach different traits to a group described as dialect speakers. A usage condition can test whether the same tendencies arise when the model encounters dialectal language without an explicit group label. The comparison also permits an analysis of whether demographic naming and linguistic realization contribute independently or interactively to model behavior. Matched dialect–standard sentence pairs are especially useful for this purpose because they reduce differences in propositional content while preserving the linguistic cue of interest.

The present work builds on these strands of research by treating German dialect bias as a joint problem of social association and model decision making. It evaluates multiple regional varieties rather than using dialect as a single undifferentiated category, and it distinguishes explicit references to dialect speakers from implicit cues provided by dialect usage. In doing so, the study connects sociolinguistic accounts of dialect attitudes with contemporary methods for measuring representational and decision bias in large language models.

title: Large Language Models Discriminate Against Speakers of G erman Dialects
text:
## Methodology

### Research Design

We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) associate German dialect speakers with socially undesirable characteristics and whether these associations affect model decisions. The evaluation distinguishes between two related forms of bias. **Dialect naming bias** refers to differences in model responses when a speaker is explicitly identified as a German dialect speaker. **Dialect usage bias** refers to differences elicited by dialectal language itself, without explicitly naming the speaker’s linguistic background.

The study uses two complementary evaluation paradigms. In the **association task**, models are prompted to associate speakers with adjectives describing socially relevant traits. In the **decision task**, models make judgments involving a target person whose linguistic background is manipulated through either an explicit demographic label or dialect usage. Comparisons with standard German controls allow us to separate responses to dialect information from responses to the semantic content of the prompts.

### Sociolinguistic Trait Dimensions

The trait dimensions evaluated in the study were derived from recurring characterizations of dialect speakers in sociolinguistic research. These dimensions cover both socially desirable and undesirable perceptions, including interpersonal, intellectual, social, and status-related characteristics. For each dimension, the evaluation uses adjective pairs or adjective sets that permit comparisons between favorable and unfavorable associations.

The same conceptual trait dimensions are used across the association and decision tasks where possible. This alignment makes it possible to assess whether patterns observed in direct adjective associations are also reflected in model judgments. Adjectives are presented in a balanced manner so that positive and negative evaluations are not confounded with a particular wording or response format.

### Models and Prompting Procedure

We evaluate a set of contemporary LLMs capable of processing German-language prompts. The models are tested under standardized prompting conditions, with identical instructions and response formats across dialect conditions whenever technically possible. Prompts are written in German and are designed to minimize irrelevant variation in syntax, length, topic, and discourse context.

For each task, the linguistic condition is varied while all other prompt components are held constant. The primary conditions are:

1. **Explicit-label condition:** the target is described as a speaker of a German dialect.
2. **Dialect-usage condition:** the target produces or is associated with a sentence written in a regional German dialect, without an explicit label identifying the speaker as a dialect speaker.
3. **Standard-German control condition:** the target produces a meaning-equivalent sentence in standard German.
4. **Neutral control condition, where applicable:** the target is described without information about dialect use or linguistic identity.

This design permits separate estimates of bias associated with naming a linguistic demographic and bias associated with the linguistic form of the target’s utterance. Prompts are evaluated independently, and model outputs are recorded without post-processing beyond the extraction of the requested response.

### Association Task

The association task measures the adjectives that models associate with speakers under different linguistic conditions. Each prompt presents a target person or speaker and asks the model to select, rank, or provide descriptors corresponding to the predefined trait dimensions. The target is manipulated across the explicit-label, dialect-usage, and control conditions.

For each model and condition, responses are coded according to whether they express favorable or unfavorable evaluations on the relevant trait dimensions. When models generate free-text responses, the outputs are mapped to the predefined adjective categories using a consistent coding scheme. Responses that do not address the requested trait or cannot be assigned reliably to a category are treated as non-informative rather than being interpreted as positive or negative evidence.

Dialect naming bias is estimated by comparing the distribution of positive and negative associations in the explicit-label condition with the relevant control condition. Dialect usage bias is estimated by comparing responses to dialect sentences with responses to meaning-matched standard German sentences. These comparisons are conducted separately for each model and trait dimension and are also summarized across dimensions.

### Dialect Evaluation Corpus

To measure bias elicited by dialect usage, we construct a parallel corpus containing sentences from seven regional German dialects and corresponding standard-German versions. The dialect sentences represent naturally occurring or dialectologically appropriate regional language patterns, while the standard-German counterparts preserve the propositional content of the dialect sentences as closely as possible.

Each dialect sentence is paired with a standard-German sentence that conveys the same meaning. The pairs are designed to reduce confounding from lexical content, sentence topic, and communicative function. Where dialectal forms require structural changes, the standard-German counterpart is adjusted to remain grammatical and semantically equivalent rather than being produced through word-for-word substitution.

The corpus includes examples from multiple regional varieties, including Alemannic and Bavarian, and is used to compare model judgments across dialects as well as against the standard-language baseline. Dialect identity is retained for analysis, but the primary comparison concerns the difference between dialect and standard-German realizations of the same content.

### Decision Task

The decision task examines whether linguistic information influences model judgments beyond direct adjective association. Models are presented with otherwise comparable descriptions of a target person or situation and are asked to make a decision or evaluation relevant to the trait dimensions under study. The target’s linguistic identity is manipulated through explicit labeling, dialect usage, or standard-German usage.

The decision prompts use matched scenarios across conditions. Information unrelated to language, such as the target’s actions, qualifications, or situational context, is held constant. The response format is constrained where possible—for example, through a specified choice, rating, or ranking format—to facilitate comparison across conditions. If a model provides an explanation in addition to the requested decision, the decision itself is analyzed separately from the explanatory text.

Decision bias is operationalized as a systematic difference in the likelihood of receiving a favorable or unfavorable outcome across linguistic conditions. Comparisons between the explicit-label and control conditions measure dialect naming bias in decision making, whereas comparisons between dialect and standard-German versions measure dialect usage bias.

### Bias Measures

For each model, task, dialect condition, and trait dimension, we calculate the relative frequency or average strength of favorable and unfavorable responses. Bias is measured through contrasts between matched conditions rather than through the absolute presence of any single adjective or decision. A negative contrast indicates that the dialect-associated condition receives less favorable treatment than its corresponding control.

The analysis distinguishes three comparisons:

- **Naming contrast:** explicit identification of the target as a German dialect speaker versus a linguistically unspecified or otherwise matched target.
- **Usage contrast:** a dialect sentence versus its meaning-equivalent standard-German counterpart.
- **Amplification contrast:** the difference between the naming contrast and the usage contrast, indicating whether explicit demographic labeling produces a stronger effect than dialect usage alone.

Results are examined at the level of individual models, dialects, and trait dimensions before being aggregated across the evaluation. This procedure makes it possible to determine whether observed effects are concentrated in particular dialects or traits or instead reflect a broader pattern across the test set.

### Statistical Analysis

The statistical analysis compares model responses across matched prompt conditions. Because the observations are generated from paired linguistic materials, the primary comparisons are conducted within sentence or scenario pairs wherever applicable. Uncertainty is estimated using resampling or other appropriate inferential procedures, with adjustments applied when multiple trait dimensions or dialect conditions are evaluated simultaneously.

We report effect directions and magnitudes for the naming and usage contrasts rather than relying solely on aggregate response frequencies. The analysis also examines consistency across models and dialects. A bias pattern is considered robust when it is reproduced across multiple matched items and remains evident across the evaluated models or model families, rather than being driven by a small number of prompts.

### Reproducibility and Response Processing

All models receive the same task instructions, condition-specific manipulations, and response constraints to the extent permitted by their interfaces. Prompt templates, corpus items, condition labels, and response-coding rules are maintained separately from the model outputs. Generated responses are preserved in their original form, and any transformations used for analysis are applied uniformly across conditions.

The evaluation does not treat dialect use as an indicator of speaker ability, identity, or social status. Instead, dialect and standard-German conditions are used as controlled linguistic stimuli for measuring differences in model associations and decisions.

title: Large Language Models Discriminate Against Speakers of G erman Dialects
text:
## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Research questions and experimental conditions

Our experiments address three questions. First, do LLMs associate German dialect speakers with the negative social characteristics documented in the sociolinguistic literature? Second, do these associations affect model decisions when dialect information is relevant to a task? Third, does bias differ depending on whether dialect identity is stated explicitly or inferred from dialect usage?

To separate these effects, we evaluate two forms of dialect information. In the **dialect-naming condition**, prompts explicitly identify an individual as a German dialect speaker. In the **dialect-usage condition**, the individual is represented through a sentence written in a regional dialect, without an explicit demographic label. Standard German counterparts are used as matched controls wherever possible. The two conditions therefore distinguish bias triggered by an explicit linguistic-group label from bias triggered by the linguistic form of an utterance itself.

All models are evaluated with the same task formulations and controlled prompt structure. Apart from the manipulated dialect information, the linguistic and situational content of paired examples is held constant. This design allows differences in model outputs to be attributed to dialect naming or dialect usage rather than to unrelated semantic content.

### 4.2 Models and prompting procedure

We evaluate a set of contemporary large language models using their text-generation or instruction-following interfaces. The models are presented with identical task instructions, stimuli, and response options, subject to the formatting requirements of each model interface. We do not provide models with definitions of the dialects or with information about the social stereotypes under investigation.

For generative responses, outputs are constrained to the response format required by the respective task whenever the interface permits such control. Responses that do not follow the specified format are treated separately from valid responses rather than being interpreted as evidence for either dialect condition. We repeat each evaluation under consistent sampling settings and aggregate responses at the stimulus level. The primary comparisons are within-model comparisons between dialect and standard German conditions.

### 4.3 Association task

The association task measures whether models connect dialect speakers with socially evaluative characteristics. Each prompt describes a target person using either an explicit dialect label or a dialect sentence and asks the model to select or generate adjectives associated with that person. Matched prompts replace the dialect information with standard German wording while preserving the surrounding context.

The adjective inventory is based on traits discussed in the sociolinguistic literature on perceptions of German dialect speakers. We distinguish negatively and positively valenced associations and examine both the overall distribution of adjective choices and the relative frequency with which particular traits are assigned to dialect versus standard German conditions. The analysis focuses on systematic differences across matched stimuli rather than on isolated model responses.

We define **dialect naming bias** as a greater tendency to produce negative associations when a person is explicitly described as a dialect speaker than when the corresponding control description is used. We define **dialect usage bias** in the association task as a greater tendency to produce negative associations in response to dialect usage than in response to the standard German counterpart. These measures are computed separately for each model and condition, allowing us to determine whether the pattern is consistent across models and dialects.

### 4.4 Decision task

The decision task examines whether the associations observed in the previous experiment influence model behavior in a more consequential setting. Models are given scenarios involving individuals characterized either by an explicit dialect label or by dialect usage. They must make a decision between matched alternatives, such as selecting or evaluating one of the individuals. The alternatives are constructed so that dialect information is the relevant manipulated variable, while other available information is held constant.

We assess the proportion of decisions that disadvantage the dialect condition relative to its standard German counterpart. Decisions are analyzed separately for explicitly named speakers and for speakers represented through dialect usage. The resulting measures capture **dialect naming bias** and **dialect usage bias** in decision making, respectively. In addition to aggregate comparisons, we examine whether the direction of the effect is stable across models and across the regional dialects included in the evaluation corpus.

### 4.5 Dialect evaluation corpus

To evaluate dialect usage, we construct a paired corpus containing sentences from seven regional German dialects, including Alemannic and Bavarian, together with standard German counterparts. Each dialect sentence is paired with a semantically corresponding sentence in standard German. The corpus is designed to preserve propositional content while retaining the linguistic features that distinguish the regional varieties.

The corpus is used in both association and decision experiments. In each case, a dialect sentence and its standard German counterpart are inserted into otherwise equivalent prompts. This paired design reduces the influence of topic, sentence meaning, and prompt context. It also permits comparisons both across dialects and between dialect usage and explicit dialect naming.

Because dialects differ in their orthographic conventions and in the extent to which they are represented in written resources, we interpret results at the level of systematic model behavior rather than as a measure of linguistic distance between varieties. The evaluation is intended to test reactions to regional German language use, not to establish a single canonical spelling system for any dialect.

### 4.6 Statistical analysis

For each model, we compare responses to matched dialect and standard German stimuli. Association outcomes are summarized by the relative presence of negative and positive adjectives, while decision outcomes are summarized by the frequency with which the dialect-associated option is disfavored. We perform comparisons separately for explicit dialect naming and dialect usage and then examine whether the two forms of information produce different effect patterns.

The principal evidence for bias is a consistent directional difference between matched conditions. We additionally assess whether these differences are statistically reliable across stimuli. Results are reported at the model level and, where appropriate, aggregated across models and dialects. Since the objective is to characterize systematic model behavior, we emphasize consistency across prompts and dialects rather than relying on individual examples.

### 4.7 Experimental findings

Across the evaluated models, the association task reveals a consistent negative shift for German dialect speakers. Explicitly naming dialect speakers leads models to produce less favorable adjective associations than in the corresponding control condition. Dialect usage also elicits negative associations relative to standard German usage, demonstrating that the effect is not limited to an explicit group label.

The same pattern extends to decision making. Models more often disadvantage individuals associated with German dialects in the matched decision scenarios, both when dialect identity is stated directly and when it is conveyed through dialect usage. Thus, the observed associations are reflected not only in descriptive language but also in model choices.

Finally, the comparison between information conditions shows that explicit linguistic-demographic labeling produces stronger bias than the corresponding implicit dialect cue. This result contrasts with the expectation that explicit demographic information necessarily reduces reliance on indirect stereotypes. In the present setting, naming German dialect speakers amplifies the negative response, while dialect usage alone produces a weaker but still systematic effect.

title: Large Language Models Discriminate Against Speakers of G erman Dialects
text:
## Conclusion

This study shows that large language models can reproduce and reinforce negative stereotypes associated with speakers of German regional dialects. Across both association and decision tasks, the evaluated models exhibited dialect naming and dialect usage biases, linking dialect speakers with less favorable attributes and incorporating these associations into their judgments. These findings indicate that linguistic variation is not treated as socially neutral by current LLMs, even when the relevant demographic distinction is conveyed through language use rather than explicit identity information.

Our results further suggest that explicit references to German dialect speakers may intensify biased responses, rather than mitigating them. This pattern contrasts with observations from some prior studies of demographic bias and highlights the importance of examining linguistic identity as a distinct dimension of social bias. Evaluations that focus only on standard-language inputs or explicit demographic categories may therefore overlook important forms of discrimination encoded in model behavior.

More broadly, the findings underscore the cultural and social risks of deploying LLMs in contexts involving regional identity, education, employment, public services, or other settings in which judgments about speakers may carry material consequences. Future work should extend this analysis to additional dialects, languages, tasks, and model architectures, while also investigating the sources of these associations and methods for reducing them. Developing evaluations that represent linguistic diversity more adequately will be essential for building language technologies that do not devalue speakers because of how they speak.

title: M ol E rr2 F ix: Benchmarking LLM Trustworthiness in Chemistry via Modular Error Detection, Localization, Explanation, and Correction
