## Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to describe and reason about molecules, yet their outputs may contain subtle structural or semantic inaccuracies that are difficult to detect and repair. We introduce **MolErr2Fix**, a benchmark for evaluating the trustworthiness of LLMs in chemical language understanding through four complementary capabilities: error detection, error localization, explanation, and correction. The benchmark contains 1,193 finely annotated error instances drawn from molecular descriptions, with each instance represented by four annotations: the error category, its textual span, a rationale describing the problem, and a corrected formulation. This design enables evaluation not only of whether a model identifies an error, but also of whether it can associate the error with the appropriate text, provide chemically meaningful justification, and produce a valid revision. In contrast to benchmarks centered primarily on molecule-to-text generation or molecular property prediction, MolErr2Fix targets the verification and refinement of chemically grounded statements. Evaluations of contemporary LLMs indicate persistent limitations across these interdependent tasks, highlighting challenges in reliable chemical reasoning and self-correction. The benchmark, together with its annotations and evaluation API, will be released to support systematic comparison and future development of more dependable language models for molecular science.

title: M ol E rr2 F ix: Benchmarking LLM Trustworthiness in Chemistry via Modular Error Detection, Localization, Explanation, and Correction
text:
## 1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to process and generate scientific text, including descriptions of molecules, chemical structures, and molecular properties. Their ability to summarize technical information and produce fluent explanations creates opportunities for applications in literature analysis, education, molecular design, and scientific communication. However, fluency does not guarantee chemical validity. An LLM may generate a description that is linguistically plausible while containing an incorrect functional group, an invalid structural relationship, an inconsistent molecular interpretation, or an imprecise chemical statement. Such errors can be difficult to identify because they are often embedded in otherwise coherent text.

The reliability of LLMs in chemistry therefore depends not only on whether they can generate molecular descriptions, but also on whether they can critically evaluate them. In practical settings, a useful system should determine whether an error is present, identify the portion of text associated with the error, explain why the statement is problematic, and provide a chemically appropriate correction. These capabilities involve distinct forms of reasoning. Error detection requires judging the validity of a statement; localization requires connecting the error to a specific textual span; explanation requires articulating the underlying chemical issue; and correction requires producing a revised statement that preserves the intended meaning while removing the error. A model may succeed at one of these steps while failing at another, making aggregate assessments insufficient for diagnosing its limitations.

Existing evaluations of language models in molecular science have largely emphasized molecule-to-text generation, molecular property prediction, question answering, or general knowledge assessment. Although these tasks provide important information about a model’s capabilities, they do not directly measure whether a model can verify and repair chemically flawed descriptions. In particular, they offer limited support for analyzing the relationship between an erroneous claim, its textual location, the rationale for identifying it, and the corresponding correction. The absence of such fine-grained evaluation makes it difficult to distinguish failures of chemical knowledge from failures of grounding, explanation, or revision.

To address this gap, we introduce **MolErr2Fix**, a benchmark for modular evaluation of LLM trustworthiness in chemistry. The benchmark focuses on the identification and correction of structural and semantic errors in molecular descriptions. Each annotated instance is represented by a four-part record consisting of an error type, the location of the relevant span, an explanation of the problem, and a corrected formulation. This design supports separate assessment of error detection, localization, explanation, and correction, while also enabling evaluation of their combination as an end-to-end process. The benchmark thus treats chemical verification as a set of related but distinguishable capabilities rather than as a single generation task.

MolErr2Fix contains 1,193 fine-grained error instances. Its annotations are intended to capture the kinds of inconsistencies and inaccuracies that can arise when molecular information is expressed in natural language. By pairing each error with both an explanatory rationale and a correction, the benchmark evaluates not only whether a model identifies an issue, but also whether it understands the issue sufficiently to justify and repair its judgment. This structure can support more informative comparisons among models and reveal specific weaknesses that would be obscured by binary correctness scores.

We evaluate contemporary LLMs using the benchmark’s modular tasks and examine their ability to detect, localize, explain, and correct errors in molecular descriptions. The resulting assessment highlights persistent challenges in chemically grounded reasoning and motivates evaluation protocols that go beyond surface-level fluency. MolErr2Fix is designed as a reusable resource for studying these challenges, with publicly released annotations and an evaluation API intended to facilitate reproducible research.

In summary, this work makes three contributions:

1. We introduce MolErr2Fix, a benchmark centered on trustworthiness and error correction in chemical language understanding.
2. We provide fine-grained quadruple annotations covering error type, span location, explanation, and correction across 1,193 error instances.
3. We establish a modular evaluation framework for analyzing LLM performance on chemical error detection, localization, explanation, and revision.

title: M ol E rr2 F ix: Benchmarking LLM Trustworthiness in Chemistry via Modular Error Detection, Localization, Explanation, and Correction
text:
## Related Work

### Molecular Language Understanding and Generation

Research at the intersection of natural language processing and chemistry has largely focused on connecting molecular structures with textual descriptions, scientific knowledge, and experimentally relevant information. Common tasks include molecule-to-text generation, text-to-molecule retrieval, chemical named-entity recognition, reaction information extraction, property prediction, and question answering over chemical knowledge. These tasks have supported the development of models that associate molecular representations with terminology describing functional groups, substituents, reactivity, and physicochemical properties.

A substantial body of work also studies the use of molecular representations such as SMILES strings, molecular graphs, fingerprints, and learned structural embeddings. These representations enable models to perform structure-aware prediction and generation, but they do not by themselves guarantee that a generated textual description is chemically valid. In particular, a description may contain a plausible-sounding but incorrect statement about atom connectivity, stereochemistry, functional groups, or molecular properties. Existing molecule-to-text and chemistry question-answering settings often evaluate the final answer as a whole, which can obscure the specific source and nature of an error.

### Chemical Reasoning and Scientific Factuality

Recent work has investigated the capacity of pretrained language models and LLMs to answer chemistry questions, interpret molecular structures, and carry out multi-step scientific reasoning. Although these models can produce fluent and contextually appropriate responses, fluency is not a reliable indicator of chemical correctness. Errors may arise from confusion between related chemical concepts, incorrect interpretation of structural notation, unsupported inferences, or failure to distinguish explicitly stated information from chemically implied properties.

This challenge is related to broader research on factuality, hallucination detection, and verifiable generation in scientific domains. Existing approaches commonly assess whether an answer agrees with a reference, retrieved source, symbolic tool, or external knowledge base. Such evaluations are useful for measuring overall correctness, but they often treat an erroneous response as a single unit. For chemistry, this level of abstraction is insufficient when a response contains several claims with different statuses, or when only a localized phrase is inconsistent with the underlying molecular structure. Fine-grained assessment therefore requires not only determining whether an error exists, but also identifying its location, explaining why it is incorrect, and proposing a chemically valid revision.

### Error Detection, Attribution, and Correction

In natural language processing, error analysis and text correction have been studied in areas such as grammatical error correction, misinformation detection, fact verification, and hallucination mitigation. These tasks have motivated datasets that annotate incorrect spans, categorize error types, and provide corrected alternatives. Such modular formulations offer more informative diagnostics than binary correctness judgments because they separate recognition of an error from the reasoning needed to repair it.

Scientific and technical text introduces additional difficulties. Errors are often domain-specific, locally expressed, and dependent on structured knowledge that is not fully recoverable from linguistic context alone. In molecular descriptions, for example, a single incorrect term can alter the interpretation of a functional group or imply an impossible structural relationship. Conversely, a statement may be linguistically well formed and broadly plausible while remaining inconsistent with the described molecule. Effective evaluation must consequently account for both semantic content and molecular structure.

Prior correction-oriented systems have frequently focused on producing a fluent replacement or selecting the correct answer from predefined alternatives. These settings provide limited insight into whether a model can justify its decision or distinguish between different failure modes. A benchmark that jointly evaluates detection, localization, explanation, and correction can expose these intermediate capabilities and clarify whether a model fails because it overlooks an error, identifies the wrong span, misunderstands the chemical issue, or cannot formulate an appropriate repair.

### Evaluation of LLMs in Chemistry

The emergence of instruction-tuned LLMs has expanded the scope of chemistry evaluation beyond conventional prediction tasks. Models are now assessed on chemical question answering, reaction reasoning, molecular interpretation, synthesis planning, and scientific dialogue. These evaluations demonstrate the usefulness of general-purpose language models while also highlighting limitations in consistency, grounding, multi-step reasoning, and resistance to confident but unsupported answers.

Many existing evaluations emphasize task-level accuracy, exact-match performance, or preference-based judgments. Such metrics are valuable for comparing systems, but they provide limited information about the internal structure of a response-level failure. They may also reward an answer that reaches the correct conclusion for an incorrect reason, or penalize a chemically acceptable answer because of surface-level differences from a reference. For molecular descriptions, evaluation is further complicated by the need to recognize equivalent formulations, distinguish structural from semantic mistakes, and assess whether a proposed correction preserves the intended meaning.

MolErr2Fix is positioned within this broader movement toward diagnostic and trustworthy evaluation. Rather than measuring only whether an LLM can generate or answer a chemistry-related statement, it evaluates a sequence of related competencies: recognizing that a description is problematic, pinpointing the relevant text, characterizing the underlying error, and producing a corrected description. This formulation is intended to make model behavior more interpretable and to provide a focused test of the chemical verification abilities required for reliable molecular communication.

title: M ol E rr2 F ix: Benchmarking LLM Trustworthiness in Chemistry via Modular Error Detection, Localization, Explanation, and Correction
text:
## 2. Methodology

### 2.1 Benchmark Objective and Task Formulation

MolErr2Fix is designed to evaluate whether a language model can identify and repair errors in natural-language descriptions of molecules. The benchmark decomposes this capability into four related subtasks:

1. **Error detection:** determine whether a molecular description contains a chemically or semantically problematic statement.
2. **Error localization:** identify the text span associated with the error.
3. **Error explanation:** describe why the identified content is incorrect or misleading.
4. **Error correction:** produce a revised description that resolves the error while preserving the intended chemical meaning.

This decomposition separates recognizing an error from understanding its source and generating an appropriate repair. It also permits models to be evaluated either as complete error-correction systems or as components within a modular verification pipeline.

Each benchmark instance is represented by a molecular description together with a structured annotation
\[
(e, s, x, c),
\]
where \(e\) denotes the error type, \(s\) is the erroneous span or its location, \(x\) is an explanation of the error, and \(c\) is the corresponding correction. The original description is retained as the context for all four subtasks. Depending on the evaluation setting, a model may receive only the description or may be asked to solve the subtasks sequentially.

### 2.2 Data Representation

The benchmark focuses on descriptions that communicate molecular structure, chemical properties, or chemically relevant relationships in natural language. The unit of annotation is an error instance rather than an entire document. Consequently, a single description can support one or more independently evaluated error instances when it contains multiple distinct issues.

Errors are organized into categories that capture both **structural** and **semantic** failures. Structural errors concern statements that are incompatible with the molecular representation or with chemically relevant structural information. Semantic errors concern incorrect interpretation, attribution, or description of molecular features and relationships. The category inventory is used to standardize annotation and to enable category-specific analysis without reducing all failures to a binary notion of correctness.

For every instance, the annotation records:

- the error category;
- the character- or token-level span associated with the error;
- a natural-language rationale explaining the chemical or semantic inconsistency;
- a corrected formulation or replacement.

The correction is expected to address the annotated problem directly and to retain information from the original description whenever that information is not itself erroneous. This design distinguishes minimal error repair from unrestricted rewriting.

### 2.3 Annotation Protocol

Annotation is conducted at the level of fine-grained error instances. Annotators first examine the molecular description and identify claims that may be inconsistent with the intended molecular structure or with established chemical meaning. They then assign an error category, mark the smallest span that adequately expresses the problematic content, explain the basis of the error, and formulate a corrected version.

The annotation guidelines emphasize three principles. First, an error must be grounded in the chemical content of the description rather than in stylistic preference alone. Second, the selected span should support unambiguous localization and should avoid including unaffected context. Third, explanations and corrections should be sufficiently explicit to make the intended repair independently interpretable.

The resulting benchmark contains **1,193 annotated error instances**, each associated with the four-part annotation described above. The annotations are intended to support both independent evaluation of each capability and joint evaluation of the full detection-to-correction process. In settings where an instance contains multiple possible interpretations, the annotation framework prioritizes chemically defensible explanations and corrections that are consistent with the underlying molecular description.

### 2.4 Modular Evaluation Tasks

MolErr2Fix evaluates models through four modules.

#### Error detection

For detection, the model predicts whether the supplied description contains an error. In a finer-grained setting, it may also identify the category of the error. This task measures a model’s ability to distinguish chemically problematic content from valid molecular statements.

#### Error localization

Given a description containing an error, the model identifies the corresponding span. Predictions may be represented as character offsets, token offsets, or quoted text, provided that they can be mapped back to the original description. Localization is evaluated independently from explanation and correction so that a model is not rewarded for generating a plausible repair when it fails to identify the source of the problem.

#### Error explanation

The model generates a rationale describing the nature of the error. An acceptable explanation should connect the problematic statement to the relevant chemical or semantic constraint. Explanations are therefore assessed for correctness and relevance rather than for lexical similarity alone. Evaluation may combine reference-based comparison with structured criteria, such as whether the explanation identifies the appropriate error type and addresses the localized content.

#### Error correction

For correction, the model rewrites the erroneous portion or provides a corrected description. A valid correction should remove the identified error, remain consistent with the molecular context, and avoid introducing additional inaccuracies. The correction task is evaluated separately from grammatical fluency, since a linguistically well-formed revision is not sufficient if its chemical content remains incorrect.

The four modules can also be composed into an end-to-end setting. In that setting, the model first determines whether an error is present, localizes it, explains the underlying issue, and finally generates a corrected description. Modular scores reveal where a system fails, whereas end-to-end assessment measures whether these capabilities work together in a realistic verification workflow.

### 2.5 Evaluation Criteria

The evaluation protocol uses task-appropriate measures. Detection is assessed using classification metrics that account for correct and incorrect error decisions, with category prediction evaluated when applicable. Localization is assessed by comparing predicted and gold spans using overlap- or boundary-based criteria. This makes it possible to distinguish an exact match from a prediction that captures only part of the relevant phrase.

Explanation quality is assessed according to the factual adequacy of the rationale, its correspondence to the annotated error, and its usefulness for justifying the correction. Because chemically equivalent explanations can use different wording, lexical matching alone is insufficient. Correction quality is assessed by checking whether the proposed revision resolves the annotated issue while preserving the intended molecular meaning. Where appropriate, correction assessment also considers whether the output introduces a new structural or semantic error.

In addition to aggregate scores, evaluation is performed by error category and by module. This enables analysis of whether a model is better at recognizing structural inconsistencies than semantic ones, whether localization is a bottleneck for subsequent correction, and whether explanations provide chemically meaningful justification. The benchmark’s evaluation API standardizes output parsing and metric computation, allowing systems that use different prompting or generation strategies to be compared under a common protocol.

### 2.6 Benchmark Usage

MolErr2Fix is intended to support controlled comparisons among language models, prompting strategies, and externally augmented systems. Models may be evaluated in zero-shot, few-shot, or fine-tuned settings, provided that their outputs are converted to the benchmark’s structured format. A system can therefore be analyzed at multiple levels: as a detector of unreliable chemical statements, as a localizer of the relevant text, as an explanatory reasoner, or as a complete correction system.

The benchmark is deliberately organized around observable intermediate outputs. This design makes it possible to diagnose whether an apparently successful correction results from genuine identification of the error or from unsupported text generation. It also provides a basis for studying the relationship between chemical verification, explanation, and reliable revision in language models.

title: M ol E rr2 F ix: Benchmarking LLM Trustworthiness in Chemistry via Modular Error Detection, Localization, Explanation, and Correction
text:
## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental objectives and task formulation

We evaluate whether contemporary large language models can reliably identify and repair errors in molecular descriptions. MolErr2Fix supports four related subtasks:

1. **Error detection:** determine whether a molecular description contains a chemically or semantically incorrect statement.
2. **Error localization:** identify the text span associated with the error.
3. **Error explanation:** describe why the identified statement is problematic.
4. **Error correction:** revise the description so that it is chemically and linguistically appropriate.

Each example is annotated with an error type, an error span, an explanation, and a corrected form. The experiments evaluate the subtasks independently and jointly. In the independent setting, the model receives the original description and is asked to perform one task at a time. In the joint setting, it produces the complete structured output corresponding to the annotated quadruple. This distinction allows us to separate failures in individual capabilities from errors introduced when the model must perform detection, localization, explanation, and correction simultaneously.

The benchmark includes both structural and semantic error categories. Structural errors concern properties or relations that conflict with the molecular structure, whereas semantic errors include incorrect terminology, implausible descriptions, and statements whose interpretation is inconsistent with the intended chemical meaning. This mixture is intended to test whether a model can move beyond surface-level proofreading and perform chemically informed verification.

### 4.2 Evaluated systems and prompting protocol

We evaluate a set of current general-purpose and chemistry-oriented LLMs. The models are tested using their standard inference interfaces, without task-specific parameter updates, unless a separately specified supervised setting is used. This design measures the degree to which existing systems can apply their pretrained linguistic and chemical knowledge to fine-grained error analysis.

For each model, the input consists of a molecular description and a task instruction. For joint evaluation, the instruction requires a structured response containing the predicted error type, the corresponding text span, an explanation, and a corrected description. The required output format is fixed across models to facilitate automatic parsing and comparison. Models are instructed not to introduce unrelated changes to descriptions that are already correct and to preserve chemically relevant information when proposing corrections.

To examine the effect of decomposition, we compare two inference strategies. In the **end-to-end setting**, a single model call produces all four components of the prediction. In the **modular setting**, the model addresses the subtasks sequentially: it first determines whether an error is present, then localizes and explains the error, and finally generates a correction conditioned on the preceding outputs. The modular setting reflects the structure of MolErr2Fix and makes it possible to identify which stage contributes most strongly to an incorrect final answer. When a model does not produce a valid structured response, the corresponding fields are marked as missing rather than inferred from the surrounding text.

### 4.3 Evaluation metrics

Performance is reported separately for each annotation component and for the complete quadruple.

For error detection, we measure classification performance using precision, recall, and F1, with results reported for both the overall benchmark and individual error categories where sufficient examples are available. Localization is evaluated by comparing predicted spans with gold spans using exact matching and overlap-based criteria. The latter accounts for cases in which a model identifies the relevant phrase but differs slightly in its span boundaries.

Error explanations are assessed for their agreement with the annotated rationale. Because explanations may be valid despite substantial wording differences, evaluation considers both semantic adequacy and whether the response identifies the underlying chemical or semantic issue. The evaluation protocol distinguishes explanations that correctly identify the problem from explanations that merely restate the proposed correction or make an unsupported claim.

Corrections are evaluated for their agreement with the reference revision and for preservation of the intended molecular meaning. Exact textual agreement is reported when applicable, but it is not treated as the sole criterion because multiple chemically equivalent phrasings may be acceptable. Invalid, incomplete, or contradictory revisions are counted as correction failures. For joint prediction, a prediction is considered fully correct only when its error type, localization, explanation, and correction satisfy the corresponding evaluation criteria. This strict measure captures the difficulty of producing a complete and internally consistent analysis.

All scores are computed using the released evaluation interface whenever possible. In addition to aggregate performance, we examine error-type-specific results, invalid-output rates, and the propagation of mistakes across the modular pipeline. These analyses are important because a model may obtain reasonable detection scores while failing to provide a usable explanation or chemically sound correction.

### 4.4 Experimental comparisons

The main comparison is between model performance on the four individual subtasks and performance under joint evaluation. This comparison tests whether success at error detection transfers to localization, explanation, and correction. We also compare modular and end-to-end prompting to determine whether explicit decomposition improves reliability.

Further analyses examine the following factors:

- **Error category:** whether structural and semantic errors exhibit different difficulty profiles;
- **Output component:** whether models are more reliable at identifying an error than at explaining or correcting it;
- **Span complexity:** whether errors involving short, explicit phrases are easier to localize than errors expressed through longer molecular descriptions;
- **Consistency across outputs:** whether the predicted explanation supports the proposed correction and whether the correction addresses the localized span;
- **Failure behavior:** whether models appropriately abstain or report uncertainty when a description is correct, rather than introducing unnecessary revisions.

For models that support multiple inference configurations, we hold the task instructions and output schema constant while varying only the relevant decoding or prompting condition. This reduces the possibility that differences in performance arise from changes in task specification rather than from the model or evaluation setting itself.

### 4.5 Results and qualitative analysis

The evaluation reveals a clear separation between recognizing that a description may be problematic and producing a complete, chemically justified repair. Contemporary LLMs generally show stronger behavior on broad error detection than on the combined requirements of precise localization, chemically grounded explanation, and faithful correction. Performance also varies across error categories, indicating that linguistic fluency alone is insufficient for reliable molecular verification.

The modular experiments provide a more detailed view of these limitations. Errors introduced during detection or span selection can propagate to the explanation and correction stages, while apparently correct detections may still be followed by explanations that do not identify the relevant chemical principle. In other cases, models generate fluent revisions that alter information outside the erroneous span or fail to resolve the original inconsistency. These failure modes motivate evaluating the four annotation components separately rather than relying only on a single correction score.

Qualitative inspection further indicates that models may use superficially plausible terminology without establishing whether the claim is compatible with the molecular structure. This is particularly problematic for descriptions involving chemical relationships, functional-group assignments, or structural distinctions that require more than local textual matching. The benchmark therefore exposes weaknesses that are difficult to observe in conventional molecule-to-text or property-prediction evaluations.

Overall, the experiments support the use of MolErr2Fix as a diagnostic benchmark for trustworthy chemical language understanding. Its quadruple annotations make it possible to determine not only whether a model produces an incorrect answer, but also where the reasoning process fails: in recognizing the error, identifying its location, articulating its cause, or constructing an appropriate correction.

title: M ol E rr2 F ix: Benchmarking LLM Trustworthiness in Chemistry via Modular Error Detection, Localization, Explanation, and Correction
text:
## Conclusion

We introduced MolErr2Fix, a benchmark for evaluating the trustworthiness of LLMs in chemical language understanding. Rather than assessing only whether a model can generate molecular descriptions or predict molecular properties, the benchmark examines whether it can detect, localize, explain, and correct errors in such descriptions. Its fine-grained annotations provide a unified basis for studying these complementary capabilities and for distinguishing surface-level correction from chemically grounded reasoning.

Evaluation with current state-of-the-art LLMs indicates that reliable performance across the full error-resolution process remains challenging. In particular, identifying an error does not necessarily imply that a model can accurately locate its source, articulate the underlying chemical issue, or propose a valid correction. These gaps highlight the importance of modular evaluation when assessing model reliability in scientific settings.

MolErr2Fix offers a focused testbed for developing and comparing methods for chemically informed verification and revision. The release of its annotations and evaluation API is intended to support reproducible research and facilitate progress toward more dependable language models for molecular science. Future work may extend the benchmark to broader chemical domains, more diverse molecular representations, and multimodal or interactive verification settings, while also exploring methods that combine language-model reasoning with external chemical knowledge and computational validation.
